title: The Finely Wrought Urjuza
intro: Ali ibn al-Jahm set the history of the world in verse, from the creation of Adam to the accession of the caliph al-Musta'in in 248 AH (862 CE), a year before the poet's own death. It is a muzdawija in rajaz: the two halves of each line rhyme with each other and the rhyme changes from line to line, the form Arabic used for long teaching poems. The literary historian Shawqi Dayf describes it as running to “more than three hundred lines, which he made in two parts”: the first on the beginning of creation, the prophets and the vanished nations, drawn from the Quran, the Torah and the chroniclers; the second on the Prophet and the caliphs, Rightly Guided, Umayyad and Abbasid, each reign counted in years and months. In Dayf's view the second part was something new, since “the poets before him had not thought of putting this history into verse”. Khalil Mardam Bek printed it at the end of the poet's diwan as al-Muhabbara fi al-tarikh, “the finely wrought, on history”, correcting the al-Mukhbira, “the informing”, of his manuscript.

translation: Praise be to God, who brings back and who begins,
praise in abundance: He is worthy of praise.
1.sharh: He opens with praise of God, who begins creation and brings it back after death, and who alone deserves praise. The two titles echo the Quran: “It is He who begins and brings back” (85:13).

translation: Then blessings, first and last,
on the Prophet, inwardly and outwardly.
2.sharh: Then he calls down blessings on the Prophet at the beginning and at the end, in his heart and aloud. The poem closes with this same line, so the blessing frames the whole history.

translation: You who ask me how creation began,
asking as one who seeks the truth:
3.sharh: He addresses someone who has asked him how creation began, and asked in earnest, to learn the truth rather than to argue. The whole poem is framed as the answer.

translation: Trustworthy people told me,
men of learning, men of dignified bearing,
4.sharh: His sources, he says, are trustworthy men of learning and of dignified bearing. Like a historian, he vouches for his informants before he tells a single story.

translation: who led the way in seeking out the old reports
and knew the truth of the accounts,
5.sharh: These informants were foremost in seeking out what had been handed down about past nations, and they knew which accounts were true and which were not.

translation: who understood the Torah and the Gospel
and mastered the revelation and its meaning:
6.sharh: They had studied the Torah and the Gospel and mastered the Quran and its interpretation. His history, like the Muslim chronicles after it, draws on Jewish and Christian scripture as well as the Quran.

translation: that He who does whatever He wills,
to whom belong might and everlastingness,
7.sharh: What they told him begins here: that God, who does whatever He wills and to whom alone belong might and everlastingness, did what the next line tells. The sentence runs on into line 8.

translation: made Adam, bringing him into being,
and cut from him his wife, Eve,
8.sharh: God made Adam out of nothing, with no father or mother, and cut his wife Eve out of him: the tradition is that she was made from one of his ribs while he slept.

translation: beginning it on a Friday;
and when He had finished making him,
9.sharh: Adam's making began on a Friday, as a hadith says: Friday is the day Adam was created, the day he entered the Garden and the day he left it. The sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: He settled him and his wife in the Garden,
and with the two of them it went as it went.
10.sharh: God settled Adam and his wife in the Garden, and then came what came. The deliberately vague phrase points to the forbidden tree, a story too well known to need telling.

translation: Iblis deceived them, and they were taken in,
as God has made plain in His Book.
11.sharh: Iblis deceived them and they let themselves be deceived, eating from the tree they had been forbidden, as God makes plain in the Quran, where the story is told in three suras.

translation: The accursed one lured them into what they did,
and both were sent down from it to the earth.
12.sharh: The accursed one led them on into what they did, and they were both sent down from the Garden to the earth. “He led them on by deceit” is the Quran's own phrase (7:22).

translation: The old man, our father Adam, came down
on a mountain in India called Wasim.
13.sharh: Adam, father of us all, came down on a mountain in India called Wasim. Al-Tabari reports the same from the people of the Torah: Adam was sent down in India, onto a mountain of that name.

translation: How poor the exchange he took for the Garden
and for nearness to the bountiful King.
14.sharh: What a poor exchange Adam made for the Garden and for nearness to God, the bountiful King: he gave up paradise for the hardships of the earth.

translation: Weakness is in the nature of man,
above all at the beginning of time.
15.sharh: He makes an excuse for Adam: weakness is part of human nature, all the more at the dawn of time, before experience had taught anyone anything. The Quran says that “man was created weak” (4:28).

translation: They did not stay in that bliss a single day
before they took hard toil in exchange.
16.sharh: Adam and Eve did not stay in that bliss even a single day before they traded it for hard toil. Al-Maqdisi, who quotes this passage, says Adam was in the Garden only for the time between two prayers.

translation: They grew wretched, and left wretchedness
to their offspring, with worry and toil.
17.sharh: They became wretched, and passed wretchedness, worry and toil on to their descendants. It echoes God's warning to Adam about Iblis in the Quran: “Let him not drive you both from the Garden, so that you toil” (20:117).

translation: He kept asking forgiveness for his sin
until he received words from his Lord,
18.sharh: Adam kept asking forgiveness for his sin until he received words from his Lord, as the Quran says: “Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He turned to him” (2:37). The words taught him how to repent.

translation: and was safe from wrath and punishment:
God relents towards whoever repents.
19.sharh: Through his repentance Adam was safe from God's anger and punishment, for God turns in forgiveness to whoever turns to Him. The Quranic verse on Adam's repentance ends, “He is the Relenting, the Merciful” (2:37).

translation: Then they grew weary, and longed for offspring,
and Eve conceived by him.
20.sharh: Then they grew weary of being alone and longed for children, and Eve conceived by Adam: the first pregnancy on earth, and the beginning of the story of their two sons.

translation: She bore a son and a daughter, twins,
and he rejoiced that she was safe, and they were.
21.sharh: She bore a son and a daughter as twins, and Adam rejoiced that she came through safely, and the two babies too. In the traditions every birth of Eve's was a boy and a girl together.

translation: They treasured the boy, and he was named Cain,
and they saw from him what they saw.
22.sharh: They took the boy as their treasure and named him Cain, and later saw what they saw of him, when he killed his brother. “Acquired” plays on Genesis, where Cain's name is explained by Eve's words, “I have acquired a man”.

translation: Then she paused a little after him,
and bore Abel, as one of twins.
23.sharh: After a short while Eve gave birth again, and this time the boy was Abel, born like Cain together with a twin sister. Their Arabic names, Qayin and Habil, are the Bible's Cain and Abel.

translation: Abel grew to manhood, and Cain grew,
and there was no rift between them.
24.sharh: The two brothers grew up into young men, and at first there was no difference and no enmity between them. The calm of this line prepares for the jealousy that follows.

translation: They made an offering over a need,
and humbled themselves before God, and submitted.
25.sharh: Each brother offered a sacrifice to God over a matter between them, humbling himself before Him. The story is in the Quran (5:27); the traditions say the matter was which of them would marry which sister.

translation: The offering was accepted from Abel,
and Cain did not win acceptance.
26.sharh: God accepted Abel's offering, and Cain's was refused. In the traditions a fire came down from the sky and consumed Abel's sacrifice, the sign that it had been accepted.

translation: He rose, for the doom that was doomed for him,
against his brother, wrongfully, and killed him.
27.sharh: Cain rose up against his brother and killed him, wrongfully: he was driven by the doom decreed for him, and became the first killer on earth. The line plays on hayn, doom, and huyyina, was doomed.

translation: Then he lured his sister away, and they fled,
leaving a fond mother, and a father.
28.sharh: Cain then talked his sister into running away with him, and they left behind a loving mother and their father. In Genesis, Cain goes on to settle in a land east of Eden.

translation: Their home lay far from his,
and they cared nothing for the good of his nearness.
29.sharh: Cain and his sister settled far from Adam's home and turned their backs on the good of living near him. From here the poem follows two lines of descent: Seth's faithful line and Cain's errant one.

translation: God gave him Seth in return,
and he never stopped calling on God for help.
30.sharh: God gave Adam Seth in place of Abel, and Adam never stopped calling on God for help. Al-Tabari explains Seth's name as “gift of God”, because he was given in Abel's place.

translation: Until, when he sensed his death approaching,
and that was after seven hundred years,
31.sharh: When Adam felt death drawing near, seven hundred years into his life, he made Seth his heir, as the next line tells. One manuscript reads “nine hundred”, nearer to Genesis, which gives Adam 930 years.

translation: his testament went to Seth, his son;
nothing is beyond the reach of death.
32.sharh: Adam left his testament to his son Seth, making him his successor, and then he died: nothing escapes death. The second half is a general maxim that closes the story of Adam.

translation: “Worship God, and shun Cain,
and keep apart from him and his offspring.”
33.sharh: The testament: worship God, keep away from Cain, and keep apart from him and his descendants. The rest of this section turns on whether Seth's children kept that charge.

translation: Seth held to the faith,
clinging to obedience to the Merciful,
34.sharh: Seth kept the faith all his life, holding fast to obedience to God as his father had charged him. In a hadith of Abu Dharr that al-Tabari cites, Seth is one of the first messengers, with Adam, Noah and Enoch.

translation: guarding what his father had charged him with,
never overstepping it, never passing it by,
35.sharh: Seth kept his father's charge faithfully, never overstepping it and never falling short of it. The two verbs together stress how strictly he held to it.

translation: until, when his death was at hand,
and he feared his appointed time might take him unawares,
36.sharh: When Seth's death drew near and he feared his appointed hour might take him by surprise, before he had passed the charge on, he made his own testament, as the next line tells.

translation: he charged Enosh, a grown man by then,
with the same his father had charged him with before.
37.sharh: Seth passed to his son Enosh, by then a grown man, the same charge that Adam had given him. The testament now runs down Seth's line from father to son.

translation: Enosh kept following in his footsteps,
striving never to go beyond what he had bidden.
38.sharh: Enosh followed in his father's footsteps, striving never to go beyond what he had been told. The charge holds firm into the third generation, as it did in the second.

translation: Then his son Kenan followed him,
and faith was all his word and deed.
39.sharh: Enosh was followed by his son Kenan, whose every word and every deed was faith: he kept to the way of his fathers and did not swerve from it.

translation: Then Mahalalel followed Kenan,
and kept the ways his elders had laid down.
40.sharh: Kenan was succeeded by Mahalalel, who followed the ways his elders had laid down for him: the faith handed on from Seth to Enosh to Kenan.

translation: Then Jared took charge of affairs,
and Enoch, unmatched in all learning.
41.sharh: Mahalalel was succeeded by Jared, father of Enoch, and Enoch was unmatched in learning. The line is uncertain in the sources; one manuscript calls Jared “father of Khanukh”, making the relationship plain.

translation: And in his time there was Tubal,
the reckless, the misleader, the lost one,
42.sharh: In that age lived Tubal, who threw off God's rule, went astray and led others astray. Al-Tabari, citing the Torah, names Tubal of Cain's line as the man who made the first instruments of play.

translation: the first to go after amusements,
and to flaunt corruption and sin.
43.sharh: Tubal was the first to chase after amusements and the first to flaunt corruption and sin. Al-Tabari lists what he made: pipes, drums, lutes and other instruments of music.

translation: He was of the line of Cain the errant:
no wonder, a traitor born of a traitor.
44.sharh: Tubal was of the line of Cain the errant, and it is no wonder that a traitor should come from a traitor. Corruption runs in Cain's line as faith runs in Seth's.

translation: He beguiled a host of the children of Seth,
till they rebelled and violated what was forbidden,
45.sharh: Tubal led astray a great many of Seth's children, until they disobeyed God and violated what He had forbidden. Al-Tabari tells how Seth's descendants came down from their mountain and mixed with Cain's.

translation: broke the testament of their fathers,
and were seduced by amusement and by women.
46.sharh: Seth's descendants broke the testament of their fathers, which told them to keep apart from Cain's people, and were seduced by amusement and by women. The charge kept for generations was lost.

translation: Jared kept on giving his people
his counsel, and they kept blaming him,
47.sharh: Jared went on counselling his people, sparing no effort, while they heaped blame on him for it. He is the righteous elder of Seth's line who watches his own kin drift away.

translation: until, when he died, after him Idris
took up the charge, and his fire-stick struck fire.
48.sharh: When Jared died, his son Idris took up the leadership and succeeded in it. “He made his fire-stick strike fire” is an Arabic image for a man whose efforts bear fruit.

translation: He is Khanukh, if plain speech is made foreign:
may our Lord bless him and give him peace.
49.sharh: Idris is the same man as Khanukh, Enoch: the name he bears when his Arabic name is put into a foreign tongue. The poet then calls down God's blessing and peace on him as a prophet.

translation: The first to be sent to God's servants,
the first to bid them to good and right guidance,
50.sharh: Idris was the first God sent to mankind in this poem, the first to bid them to what is good and right. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Ishaq, calls him the first of Adam's descendants to be given prophethood.

translation: the first man to read and write,
who taught reckoning once he had reckoned.
51.sharh: He was the first to read and write and, once he had learnt to reckon, he taught reckoning to others. In a hadith al-Tabari cites, Enoch was the first to write with the pen, and God sent down thirty scrolls to him.

translation: Not one of his people obeyed him;
they mingled with Cain and his offspring.
52.sharh: Not one of his people obeyed him; they mingled with Cain and his descendants, breaking the testament Adam had left. The faithful line has merged into the errant one.

translation: So God raised His servant up to Himself,
once he had chosen to dwell with Him.
53.sharh: So God raised His servant Idris up to Himself, once Idris had chosen to stay with God rather than among the people who defied him. The Quran says of Idris, “We raised him to a high place” (19:57).

translation: Methuselah became the one left in charge
after Idris, the prophet, the chosen one.
54.sharh: After Idris, the chosen prophet, his son Methuselah was left in charge. In al-Tabari he is Methuselah son of Enoch, the grandfather of Noah.

translation: He warned the people of a punishment to come,
and found no one on earth who would heed,
55.sharh: Methuselah warned people of a punishment about to fall on them, and found no one anywhere on earth who would accept his warning. The punishment he foresaw is the Flood.

translation: except his son Lamech; so he charged Lamech
with a testament of piety and worship.
56.sharh: Only his son Lamech listened, so Methuselah gave Lamech a testament of piety and worship. Lamech is the father of Noah: the faithful line has narrowed to a single household.

translation: He preached to the people, and they defied him,
shied away from him and left him.
57.sharh: Lamech in turn preached to the people, and they defied him, shied away from him and left him. The age before the Flood ends with warning after warning that no one hears.

translation: Then God sent Noah to them,
a servant, true in counsel, of the One who sent him.
58.sharh: When corruption had spread everywhere, God sent them Noah, son of Lamech: a true servant of the One who sent him, and a faithful counsellor to his people. In the Quran Noah tells them, “I give you sincere counsel” (7:62).

translation: He lived a thousand years less fifty,
calling to God while the ages passed.
59.sharh: Noah lived among them for a thousand years less fifty, calling them to God while the ages went by and nothing changed. The figure is the Quran's: “He stayed among them a thousand years less fifty” (29:14).

translation: He called them in secret and called them aloud,
and it only added to their unbelief.
60.sharh: He called them in private and in public, and his calls only made them more stubborn in their unbelief. The Quran's sura of Noah describes the same: “I called them openly, and spoke to them in secret” (71:9).

translation: They sank deep in unbelief and arrogance,
and worshipped idols openly.
61.sharh: His people sank deeper into unbelief and arrogance and worshipped idols in the open. The Quran names their idols: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr (71:23).

translation: Until, when he despaired of being obeyed,
and they closed their ears against him,
62.sharh: When Noah despaired of being obeyed and they shut their ears against him, he prayed against them, as the next line tells. In the Quran they “put their fingers in their ears and wrapped themselves in their garments” (71:7).

translation: he called down ruin on them,
after he had warned them to the full.
63.sharh: Having warned them as fully as anyone could, Noah prayed for their destruction: “My Lord, do not leave a single one of the unbelievers dwelling on the earth” (71:26).

translation: He made the ark at his Lord's command,
and so came safe through, with his followers.
64.sharh: Noah built the ark at his Lord's command and so escaped with his household and his followers. The Quran: “Build the ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation” (11:37).

translation: The Flood came on, a raging water,
and left no creature on earth alive,
65.sharh: The Flood came, its water rising beyond all bounds, and left no living thing on earth. “Raging” takes up the Quran's word: “When the water rose beyond bounds, We carried you in the ship” (69:11).

translation: except those who took refuge in the ark
and were saved from the floods of destruction.
66.sharh: Only those who took refuge in the ark came through the floods of destruction. The sources disagree on how many they were: eighty, some say, others only eight, Noah and his family.

translation: All this happened in the month of Ab,
before the middle of the month, by the reckoning.
67.sharh: He dates all this to the month of Ab, August, before the middle of the month. The Quran gives no such date; it comes from the informants he named at the start of the poem.

translation: As the turmoil drew near, they resolved
to board the ark and be saved with him.
68.sharh: As the turmoil drew near, the believers resolved to board the ark and be saved with Noah. One manuscript has Noah tell “his four sons” to board, which leads into the son who refused.

translation: One of Noah's sons
defied his command and stood against him.
69.sharh: One of Noah's sons defied his father and stubbornly refused to board. In the Quran he tells Noah, “I will take refuge on a mountain that will save me from the water” (11:43).

translation: He perished among those of His servants who perished,
and the rest of his sons were saved:
70.sharh: That son perished with the rest of those who perished, and Noah's other sons were saved. In the Quran, “the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned” (11:43).

translation: Shem and Ham, and the youngest, the third,
called in the Torah Japheth.
71.sharh: The three who survived were Shem, Ham and the youngest, called Japheth in the Torah. From these three, in this telling, all the nations of the earth descend.

translation: Most of the white peoples are the seed of Shem,
most of the black peoples the seed of Ham,
72.sharh: Most of the fair-skinned peoples, he says, descend from Shem, and most of the dark-skinned from Ham. It is the division of the nations that al-Tabari and the genealogists also report.

translation: and Japheth has wonders among his seed:
Gog, the Turks and the Slavs.
73.sharh: Japheth's line includes marvels: Gog, the Turks and the Slavs. Al-Tabari likewise counts the Turks, the Slavs and Gog and Magog among the descendants of Japheth.

translation: Among the sons of Shem son of Noah are Aram,
Arpachshad, Lud and Elam.
74.sharh: Among the sons of Shem son of Noah are Aram, Arpachshad, Lud and Elam, names that come from the table of nations in Genesis. The ancient Arab peoples of the next lines trace their descent through them.

translation: After Noah the people of Ad grew many,
and mischief and corruption spread from them.
75.sharh: After Noah the people of Ad grew numerous, and mischief and corruption spread from them. Ad are the people of the prophet Hud, remembered in the Quran for their strength and their violence.

translation: Ad were of the children of Uz son of Aram,
and of the sons of Uz were Jadis and Tasm.
76.sharh: Ad descends from Uz son of Aram, and Jadis and Tasm, two lost Arab tribes, are of Uz's line too. The genealogists disagree on the descent of Jadis and Tasm.

translation: God sent Hud to them,
and he laid the truth bare for them.
77.sharh: God sent Hud to Ad, and he laid the truth bare before them, unmixed with anything else: worship God alone. His story is told in several suras of the Quran.

translation: They opposed him with the worst opposition,
and sank deep in unbelief and apostasy.
78.sharh: Ad opposed him with the worst kind of obstinacy and sank deep into unbelief and apostasy. In the Quran they tell him, “Hud, you have brought us no clear proof” (11:53).

translation: He said, “My Lord, keep the rain from them,”
and it passed them by for ten years.
79.sharh: Hud prayed his Lord to withhold the rain from them, and for ten years it passed them by; al-Tabari makes the drought three years. The drought drove Ad to send a delegation to Mecca to pray for rain.

translation: He sent a raging wind against them,
and it left not one of the house of Ad astir.
80.sharh: Then God sent a violent wind against Ad, and it left none of them walking the land. The Quran says the wind raged against them “seven nights and eight days in succession” (69:7).

translation: A delegation of seventy went out from them,
almost racing one another to Mecca.
81.sharh: Ad had sent seventy men to Mecca to pray for rain, almost racing one another to get there. Al-Tabari gives the same number. One manuscript reads “they went to Mecca to seek rain”, which says it more plainly.

translation: They prayed earnestly, raising their hands,
and Luqman son of Ad was among them.
82.sharh: The delegation prayed earnestly with their hands raised, and Luqman son of Ad was among them. He is not the wise Luqman of the Quran; al-Tabari calls him the chief of Ad.

translation: He asked for long life and great age,
and lived on until he had outlived the vultures.
83.sharh: Luqman asked for long life, and lived until he had outlived the vultures. In the tale he chose the lifespan of seven vultures, one after another; when the seventh, Lubad, died, Luqman died with it.

translation: His prayer met with an answer,
for he was not pleased with his companions.
84.sharh: Luqman's prayer was granted, because he did not approve of his companions and their unbelief. In al-Tabari he stays behind when the rest of the delegation prays, and asks for himself alone.

translation: After Ad, Thamud flourished,
and settled al-Hijr and the floor of the valley.
85.sharh: After Ad, the people of Thamud flourished and settled al-Hijr and the floor of the valley. The Quran remembers them as “Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley” (89:9).

translation: God sent Salih to them,
a youth of their own, young in years, sound of mind.
86.sharh: God sent Salih to Thamud: a young man of their own people, but of sound and weighty judgement. In the Quran his people tell him, “You were one we placed our hopes in before this” (11:62).

translation: He kept calling them until he grew old,
and only the fewest of them answered.
87.sharh: Salih kept calling his people from his youth until he was middle-aged, and only a few of them answered him. Set against “young in years” in the line before, it shows how long he preached.

translation: They brought him a smooth rock
and said, “Pray sincerely before it:
88.sharh: They brought him a smooth rock and said, “Pray sincerely before it”, as a challenge. In the traditions they demand that he bring a she-camel out of a rock as a sign that he is telling the truth.

translation: Has the One you worship any power
to make it split and bring forth a she-camel?”
89.sharh: “Has the God you worship the power to make it split open and give birth to a she-camel?” The demand is meant to trap Salih: they are sure no rock can bring forth a living creature.

translation: It split, until its hollow lay open,
with a she-camel, her foal following her.
90.sharh: The rock split open and out of it came a she-camel with her foal following behind. In the Quran Salih tells his people, “This is God's she-camel, a sign for you” (7:73).

translation: They hamstrung the she-camel, to their ruin,
and the blast of extinction struck them at once.
91.sharh: Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, and so brought on their own ruin: a deadly blast seized them without delay. The Quran gives them three days' grace and then “the Shout” takes them (11:65–67).

translation: There lies al-Hijr, emptied of Thamud:
do you see any of them left on earth?
92.sharh: Al-Hijr, Thamud's land, stands empty, and no trace of them is left on earth. The second half echoes the Quran on Ad: “Do you see any remnant of them?” (69:8). The reciter repeats this line to close the section.

translation: Then your Lord chose Abraham;
He has always been merciful to His creation.
93.sharh: After those nations perished, God chose Abraham, for He has always been merciful to His creatures and never leaves them without a guide. With Abraham a new section begins, leading through Ishmael to the Arabs.

translation: His single-hearted faith in one God was such
that he forsook the near and the far.
94.sharh: So pure was Abraham's devotion to the one God that he broke with everyone, near kin and strangers alike, when they clung to their idols, his own father included. In the Quran he says, “I will withdraw from you and from what you call on besides God” (19:48).

translation: He laid down fine laws,
and broke the idols and the images.
95.sharh: Abraham laid down good laws, some of which survive in the rites of the pilgrimage, and smashed his people's idols. The Quran tells how “he broke them into pieces, all but the biggest of them” (21:58).

translation: Lot said, “I am emigrating,
and what you command, I command my people”:
96.sharh: Lot believed in Abraham and said, “I am emigrating with you, and I will bid my people do what you bid.” The Quran: “Lot believed in him, and said, ‘I am emigrating to my Lord’” (29:26).

translation: all of which the Quran has set out;
in the Quran are truth and clear speech.
97.sharh: He leaves the story of Abraham and Lot to the Quran, which tells it in full, truthfully and clearly: there is no need to put into verse what scripture has already set out at length.

translation: God rewarded his faith,
and singled him out for argument and proof.
98.sharh: God rewarded Abraham's faith and gave him, above all others, the winning argument and clear proof against his people. The Quran: “That was Our argument, which We gave Abraham against his people” (6:83).

translation: He crushed Nimrod, the tyrant of his age,
with God's proofs and his own patience.
99.sharh: Abraham defeated Nimrod, the worst tyrant of his age, with God's arguments and his own patience. It recalls the Quran's debate in which Abraham tells the king, “God brings the sun from the east; you bring it from the west”, and the unbeliever is struck dumb (2:258).

translation: He placed wisdom in his children,
and chose them all above His servants.
100.sharh: God placed wisdom and prophethood among Abraham's descendants and chose them, every one, above all His other servants: the prophets after him come from his line. The Quran: “We placed prophethood and the Book among his offspring” (29:27).

translation: He gave the charge to Ishmael,
for he was the eldest son of the Friend.
101.sharh: Leadership after Abraham went to Ishmael, the eldest of the Friend of God's sons. Ishmael is the ancestor of the northern Arabs and of the Prophet Muhammad, towards whom the whole poem is moving.

translation: Hagar gave birth before Sarah,
and before her she was given the glad tidings
102.sharh: Hagar bore Ishmael before Sarah bore Isaac, and the glad tidings came to Hagar first. In Genesis an angel finds Hagar alone in the wilderness and announces that she will bear a son.

translation: from her Lord, and she heard a call:
“God has heard your prayer.”
103.sharh: The tidings came from her Lord, and she heard a voice tell her, “God has heard your prayer.” It follows Genesis, where the angel tells Hagar to name her son Ishmael because the Lord has heard her distress.

translation: She was settled in the secure city,
and Ishmael grew up at al-Hajun.
104.sharh: Hagar was settled in Mecca, the secure city, and Ishmael grew up near al-Hajun. The Quran preserves Abraham's prayer: “Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without crops, by Your sacred House” (14:37).

translation: One day Gabriel was there,
and the prophet Ishmael was there too,
105.sharh: One day Gabriel was there, and so was the infant Ishmael, a prophet to be. The line sets the scene for the miracle of Zamzam; the Quran calls Ishmael “a messenger, a prophet” (19:54).

translation: a little child; he cried of thirst,
and Hagar went out in search of water.
106.sharh: Ishmael was small and suffering from thirst, so Hagar went out to look for water. In the hadith she ran seven times between al-Safa and al-Marwa looking for help, a run that pilgrims still repeat.

translation: He struck the earth, and it gushed with jumjum,
boiling from his strike in rivers of water.
107.sharh: Gabriel struck the ground, and the water of Zamzam surged up, boiling out of the spot he had struck in rivers. In the hadith Gabriel dug with his heel until the water appeared, and Zamzam is still called “Gabriel's strike”.

translation: Hagar came back when she had lost hope,
and what she saw dismayed her, and she was struck dumb.
108.sharh: Hagar came back when she had given up hope of finding water, and was struck with fear at what she saw: water welling up where there had been none. She stood speechless.

translation: She began building flat stones round it;
had she left it, it would have been a running stream.
109.sharh: Hagar set about walling the water in with flat stones; had she left it alone, it would have run as a flowing spring. A hadith says the same: “God have mercy on Ishmael's mother; had she left Zamzam, it would have been a running spring.” Yaqut quotes this line without naming the poet.

translation: Jurhum came to live beside them,
wishing for kinship by marriage and for neighbourliness.
110.sharh: The tribe of Jurhum came to live beside Hagar and Ishmael, wanting to marry into the family and to share the place. In al-Bukhari's hadith they see birds circling the water, ask Hagar's leave to settle, and Ishmael later marries among them.

translation: They had daughters and sons,
a bond through mothers that ennobled the mothers' kin.
111.sharh: The marriages between Ishmael and Jurhum produced sons and daughters, so Jurhum became the maternal uncles of Ishmael's descendants: an honour for the uncles, whose sisters' sons were Abraham's line.

translation: They made Mecca their home for ages on end,
until, when they committed grave sins,
112.sharh: Jurhum lived in Mecca for ages and made it their home, until they began to commit grave sins and to violate the sanctuary; the next two lines tell what followed.

translation: and changed the law of Abraham
and made the lawful look like the forbidden,
113.sharh: They changed the religion of Abraham that Ishmael had inherited, and blurred the line between what is lawful and what is forbidden. The historians say they oppressed visitors to Mecca and devoured the Kaaba's offerings.

translation: the sons of Kinana drove them out of it,
and they left in disgrace and humiliation.
114.sharh: The tribe of Kinana drove Jurhum out of Mecca, and they left in disgrace and humiliation. The usual account names Khuza'a, with the Bakr clan of Kinana, as the tribes who fought them and drove them out.

translation: The House and the people's affairs were taken in charge
by the noblest of the sons of Ilyas.
115.sharh: After Jurhum, the Kaaba and the affairs of the people passed to the noblest descendants of Ilyas son of Mudar. The House returned to the line of Ishmael, who had built it with his father.

translation: Ishmael's law lived on
among his people, its path still clear,
116.sharh: Ishmael's religion lived on among his people, its path still clear, handed down from one generation to the next until the leadership reached Qusayy.

translation: until the charge came to Qusayy,
the Gatherer, best of the sons of Lu'ayy.
117.sharh: Leadership finally came to Qusayy, who brought Quraysh together in Mecca after they had been scattered: the best of the sons of Lu'ayy, and an ancestor of the Prophet.

translation: People yielded the Station to him,
the House, the holy sites and the sanctuary.
118.sharh: People yielded to Qusayy the Station of Abraham, the House, the holy sites and the whole sanctuary: he held every office in Mecca, from watering the pilgrims to keeping the Kaaba's keys.

translation: The bow went to the one who carved it,
and the target met its archer.
119.sharh: The charge was back with those who knew how to carry it: the bow had gone to its carver, the target had met its archer. “Give the bow to the one who carves it” is a well-known Arabic proverb.

translation: Noble ways settled deep among its people,
and pillars were raised to build them high.
120.sharh: Noble ways took deep root among the people of Mecca, and pillars were raised to hold the building up. Under Qusayy, the line says, the honour of Quraysh became a building made to last.

translation: The old man bequeathed honour to his sons,
and each of them gave, and served, and sufficed.
121.sharh: Qusayy left his honour to his sons, and every one of them was generous, useful and equal to the task. They include Abd Manaf and Abd al-Dar; Abd Manaf's son Hashim was the Prophet's great-grandfather.

translation: Hear the story of our uncle Isaac,
for I shall tell it in due order.
122.sharh: He asks the listener to hear the story of Isaac, whom he calls “our uncle”: Isaac was the brother of Ishmael, ancestor of the Arabs, so to the Arabs he is an uncle. He promises to tell it in order.

translation: He came when youth had passed
and a hundred years had gone by.
123.sharh: Isaac was born when his father's youth was long gone and a hundred years had passed over him. Genesis likewise makes Abraham a hundred years old at Isaac's birth.

translation: Through him God strengthened the Friend,
and gave support to Ishmael, the truthful.
124.sharh: Through Isaac God strengthened Abraham, the Friend, and gave support to Ishmael, the truthful: Abraham now had two prophet sons to carry on his work after him.

translation: Sarah marvelled when she was given the tidings
of him, and struck her face, and was afraid.
125.sharh: When Sarah was told she would bear Isaac, she was astonished, struck her face and was frightened, for she was old and barren. The Quran: “His wife came forward crying out, struck her face and said, ‘A barren old woman’” (51:29).

translation: She said, “How can an old woman give birth?”
She was told, “When the Mighty One decrees it.”
126.sharh: Sarah asked how an old woman could give birth, and was told: if God the Mighty decrees it. In the Quran she says, “Woe is me, shall I bear a child, an old woman, and my husband here an old man?” (11:72).

translation: And she was told that after him would come Jacob,
a word not to be denied.
127.sharh: She was told too that after Isaac would come Jacob, a word that could not prove false. The Quran: “We gave her the glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac of Jacob” (11:71).

translation: God's promise, exalted be His name, came true,
and His command overcame everything.
128.sharh: God's promise was fulfilled: Isaac was born, and Jacob after him, for God's command prevails over every other. The Quran says, “God prevails in His purpose” (12:21).

translation: Of the story of Jacob the prophet
there is what no book leaves unmentioned.
129.sharh: The story of Jacob the prophet is too well known from the scriptures and the histories to need retelling here; best known of all is his story with his son Joseph.

translation: God gave it a sura of its own,
known by Joseph's name, and famous.
130.sharh: God gave that story a sura of its own, known and famous as the sura of Joseph: the one sura of the Quran that tells a single prophet's story from beginning to end.

translation: Jacob died in the land of Egypt
after nine and ten full years.
131.sharh: Jacob died in Egypt, having lived there, the poem says, for nineteen full years. Genesis gives seventeen years for his life in Egypt.

translation: He had only come to Egypt to visit
Joseph, and then stayed on to live near him.
132.sharh: Jacob had not come to Egypt to settle: he came to visit Joseph, then stayed on to live near him until he died. The Quran: “When they came in to Joseph, he took his parents to himself” (12:99).

translation: Until, when he was sure that death was near,
he asked to be buried in Syria.
133.sharh: When Jacob knew his death was near, he asked to be buried in Syria, the land of his fathers. In Genesis he asks to lie with Abraham and Isaac in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron.

translation: Joseph carried the coffin until he buried him
in Syria, as he had bidden.
134.sharh: Joseph carried his father's coffin to Syria and buried him there, as Jacob had asked. Genesis describes a great funeral procession going up from Egypt to the family tomb.

translation: Then he went back to Egypt and lived for ages,
until he had had what he wanted of life.
135.sharh: Joseph went back to Egypt and lived there for many years, until he had had his fill of life. Genesis says he lived a hundred and ten years.

translation: Seventy of his family
had come to him with Jacob to visit.
136.sharh: Seventy members of Joseph's family had come to him with Jacob. Genesis gives the same number: all the household of Jacob that came into Egypt was seventy souls.

translation: Their number grew great in Egypt,
and there the worst of harm befell them.
137.sharh: The children of Israel multiplied in Egypt after Joseph until they were very many, and there the worst of hardships befell them. Exodus begins the same way: they were fruitful and multiplied, and a new king came to fear them.

translation: Pharaoh ruled over them by force,
and made them suffer the worst torment for ages.
138.sharh: Pharaoh ruled them by force and inflicted the worst of torments on them for a long time. The Quran: “They inflicted terrible torment on you, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women” (2:49).

translation: Then God sent Moses to them,
after He had made him holy.
139.sharh: God sent Moses to them, after He had sanctified him and chosen him for his mission. The Quran: “I am your Lord: take off your sandals, for you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa” (20:12).

translation: He freed the people from their torment;
and they were, by the reckoning, as is said,
140.sharh: Moses rescued his people from Pharaoh's torment and led them out of Egypt; as for their number, according to the reports, the next line gives it.

translation: besides the children and the feeble men:
six hundred thousand men.
141.sharh: Six hundred thousand men, not counting the children and the weak and feeble. Exodus gives the same: “about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children” (12:37).

translation: The faithful keeper of the pledge carried the coffin,
Moses, and in the coffin lay Joseph's body.
142.sharh: Moses, true to an old pledge, carried a coffin out of Egypt with Joseph's body in it. Exodus: “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the children of Israel swear an oath” (13:19).

translation: Long ages since the pledge did not deter him,
nor all the hardship he went through.
143.sharh: Neither the long years since Joseph's death nor the hardships Moses was going through kept him from carrying the body: he kept faith with a promise made generations before.

translation: Between them lay fifty-one years
and a hundred, full and well tested.
144.sharh: Between Joseph and Moses, he says, lay a hundred and fifty-one years, carefully counted. The histories disagree widely over the length of this span.

translation: They stayed forty years in the wilderness,
years such as they never lived again.
145.sharh: The Israelites wandered in the wilderness for forty years, years like no others they ever lived. The Quran: “It is forbidden them for forty years; they shall wander in the land” (5:26).

translation: Aaron son of Imran, the prophet, died
before Moses, in a sweet sleep.
146.sharh: Aaron son of Imran, the prophet, died before Moses, peacefully, as if falling asleep. In the traditions he lay down on a couch on a mountain he had climbed with Moses, and was taken there.

translation: It is said he was kept back after his brother
only for a thing decreed in the wilderness.
147.sharh: It is said that Moses outlived his brother only because of something God had decreed for the wilderness; Moses too died there. One manuscript says so plainly: “Moses died after him in the wilderness.”

translation: Then Joshua son of Nun became a prophet,
the heir of Moses, the truthful, the trusted.
148.sharh: Then Joshua son of Nun became a prophet, the heir Moses had named, truthful and trustworthy. Commentators identify him with the young man who travels with Moses in the Quran's story of al-Khidr (18:60).

translation: He waded through the deep sea of the Jordan,
and made the sea a road for him.
149.sharh: Joshua led the Israelites across the deep Jordan, and God made the water a road for him. In the Book of Joshua the river's waters stand still while the people cross on dry ground.

translation: Jericho was burned, in dread of him,
and God opened the way to conquest after conquest.
150.sharh: Jericho was burned, terrified of him, and God gave him conquest after conquest. In the Book of Joshua the walls of Jericho fall and the Israelites burn the city with fire.

translation: He said to the sun, “Stand still,” and it stood,
and he turned it from its course, and it turned back.
151.sharh: Joshua told the sun to stand still and it stood, and he turned it back from its course, so that he could finish the battle before nightfall. The story is in the Book of Joshua, and a hadith tells of a prophet, named in one version as Joshua, for whom the sun was held back.

translation: He humbled kings until they bowed,
and they were made small in his eyes, and were small.
152.sharh: Joshua humbled the kings of the land until they submitted, and God made them small in his eyes, so they counted for little. The Book of Joshua lists thirty-one kings he defeated.

translation: He settled the children of Israel in Syria,
a promise of the Merciful in revelation.
153.sharh: Joshua settled the children of Israel in Syria, fulfilling God's promise in scripture. In the Quran Moses tells his people, “Enter the holy land that God has ordained for you” (5:21).

translation: Then Caleb became a prophet, following him,
and said to the tribes, “I am going.”
154.sharh: After Joshua came Caleb, who followed in his steps as prophet and told the tribes of Israel, when his end came, “I am going.” In the Torah Caleb and Joshua are the two faithful spies Moses sent into Canaan.

translation: He left the forbearing Ezekiel,
son of the old woman, to take his place.
155.sharh: Caleb left behind him Ezekiel the forbearing, known as the son of the old woman, as his successor. Al-Tabari says his mother asked God for a child when she was old and barren, and was given him.

translation: After him the factions multiplied;
they set up their Baal, and found fault.
156.sharh: After Ezekiel the Israelites split into factions, set up their idol Baal and mocked the faith. Al-Tabari says they took an idol called Baal and worshipped it instead of God.

translation: Then Elijah son of Yasin said to them,
a prophet sent after them:
157.sharh: Elijah son of Yasin, a prophet sent to them after the prophets before him, spoke to them, as the next line tells. Al-Tabari traces his descent to Aaron; the Quran says, “Elijah too was one of the messengers” (37:123).

translation: “Worship God and cast Baal aside,”
and they grew arrogant and threatened him with death.
158.sharh: Elijah told them to worship God and throw Baal away, and they grew arrogant and threatened to kill him. In the Quran he asks them, “Do you call on Baal and forsake the best of creators?” (37:125).

translation: He went on in hiding, a wanderer,
until he was called away by death, and found rest.
159.sharh: Elijah lived in hiding, wandering from place to place, until God called him away and he found rest. Al-Tabari tells how he hid in the mountains and once sheltered with an Israelite woman, the mother of Elisha.

translation: It is said in the Torah that a horse
came to him one morning, or one evening,
160.sharh: According to the Torah, a horse came to Elijah one morning or one evening to carry him off. Al-Tabari speaks of a horse of fire; in the Book of Kings a chariot of fire and horses of fire part him from Elisha.

translation: until, when Elijah mounted it,
he vanished, and people never saw him again.
161.sharh: When Elijah mounted it he vanished, and people never learned what became of him. In al-Tabari, as the horse carries him off, Elisha calls after him, “Elijah, what do you bid me?”, and becomes his successor.

translation: Elisha, son of Akhtub, kept on
restraining them for years, and they would not be restrained.
162.sharh: Elisha son of Akhtub, Elijah's successor, spent years trying to restrain the Israelites, and they would not be restrained. The Quran names him among “the best of men” (38:48).

translation: They were robbed of the Ark after Elisha,
and Eli, their head, died of grief.
163.sharh: After Elisha the Israelites' enemies captured the Ark, and Eli, their head, died of grief at the news. Al-Tabari tells how the priest Eli fell from his seat and died when he heard the enemy had taken it. One manuscript reads instead that “their head did not rise again for grief”.

translation: Their enemies prevailed over them,
and blindness covered them after guidance.
164.sharh: Their enemies got the upper hand, and blindness came over them after they had been rightly guided: for a time they had neither a king to unite them nor a leader to follow.

translation: They asked their prophet Samuel
to plead with the majestic King for pardon.
165.sharh: The Israelites turned to their prophet Samuel and asked him to beg God, the majestic King, to forgive their stumbling and lift their defeat. Al-Tabari says Samuel had grown up in the service of Eli, the priest whose death the poem has just told.

translation: They asked him to appoint a ruler
over them, to fight their enemies.
166.sharh: Then they asked Samuel to set a ruler over them to lead them against their enemies. The Quran: “They said to a prophet of theirs, ‘Raise up a king for us, and we will fight in God's way’” (2:246).

translation: They pledged to obey his command,
to honour him and raise his standing.
167.sharh: They gave Samuel their word that they would obey the king's command, honour him and raise his standing: a promise made before they knew who he would be.

translation: God raised up Saul for them;
they followed him and went to war on Goliath.
168.sharh: God raised up Saul as their king; they followed him and marched against Goliath, the champion of their enemies. The Quran: “God has raised up Saul as king for you” (2:247).

translation: David had stayed behind
with his family, then came to him alone.
169.sharh: David had stayed behind with his family when Saul marched out, and later came to him alone. Al-Tabari makes him the youngest of thirteen brothers, who told his father that whatever he aimed at with his sling, he brought down.

translation: A solid rock spoke to him,
calling him from where the call could be heard:
170.sharh: On his way to Saul a solid rock spoke to him, calling out where he could hear it. In the traditions stones call to David as he passes, telling him to carry them, for with them he will kill Goliath.

translation: “Take me, for I am the stone of the Friend;
with me Goliath shall be killed before long.”
171.sharh: The rock said: “Take me, for I am the stone of Abraham, the Friend; with me Goliath will soon be killed.” The weapon David carries is an heirloom of the prophets, his forefathers.

translation: Before it, the stone of Isaac the prophet
had also asked him to carry it.
172.sharh: Before that, another stone, the stone of Isaac the prophet, had asked him to carry it too. David now has the stones of both Abraham and Isaac; in al-Tabari he names three stones after his forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

translation: He came to the battle in his calm,
and the stones knocked together in his bag.
173.sharh: David came to the battle calm and unhurried, and the stones clattered against each other in his bag, as if jostling to be first into the fight.

translation: Each of them longed to be the one he cast,
taking God's revenge on His enemies.
174.sharh: Each stone hoped to be the one he would cast, so that it could take God's revenge on His enemies. In this telling the stones are soldiers, each eager to be first to serve.

translation: David struck Goliath with some of them,
for they were where his end was to be looked for.
175.sharh: David struck Goliath with some of those stones, for they were where his death was to be found. The Quran: “David killed Goliath, and God gave him kingship and wisdom” (2:251).

translation: God destroyed his enemy for him,
and he won kingship and prophethood.
176.sharh: God destroyed David's enemy for him, and David won both kingship and prophethood. The Quran adds that he was given the Psalms: “To David We gave the Psalms” (4:163).

translation: Saul was envious of him,
and God gave David the victory over him.
177.sharh: Saul grew jealous of David's standing and tried to kill him, but God gave David the upper hand over him. In the traditions Saul later repented and went out to fight until he was killed.

translation: He had laid the foundations of the Holy House:
blessed be the foundation, and its founder.
178.sharh: David had laid the foundations of the Temple in Jerusalem, and the poet calls down blessings on both the foundation and its founder. The traditions, like the Book of Kings, have David begin the building and Solomon complete it.

translation: It was Solomon who completed it
after him, until the building stood.
179.sharh: It was his son Solomon who finished the building after him, until it stood complete and tall. In the Bible too, David prepares the Temple and Solomon builds it.

translation: David had charged him to complete it
when he stood on the brink of death.
180.sharh: David had charged Solomon to finish the work when he was on the point of death. As in the poem's first section, a dying father passes his charge to his son.

translation: Solomon the king held the kingdom
for some forty years, until he died.
181.sharh: Solomon the king reigned for about forty years until he died. The Book of Kings also gives him forty years; the Quran tells how he died leaning on his staff, and no one knew until a worm ate through it (34:14).

translation: Twenty of his descendants
held the kingdom after him.
182.sharh: After Solomon twenty of his descendants ruled in turn, one after another. They are the kings of Judah, Solomon's line, of the histories.

translation: Then Nebuchadnezzar took the kingdom
from them, and ruled in their place, and they were powerless.
183.sharh: Then Nebuchadnezzar took the kingdom from them and ruled in their place, and they were powerless to stop him. He was king of Babylon, and carried the Israelites off into captivity there.

translation: The wretch laid the Holy House in ruins,
and he was in love with killing souls.
184.sharh: Nebuchadnezzar, the wretch, laid the Holy House in ruins, and he delighted in killing. Commentators see him in the Quran's “servants of Ours, of terrible might” sent against Israel (17:5).

translation: He died at al-Ramla, leaving sons
to hold the kingdom after him.
185.sharh: Nebuchadnezzar died, the poem says, at al-Ramla, leaving sons who held the kingdom after him one after another, until the last of them was killed.

translation: Darius killed the last of his sons,
and their kingdom passed to him.
186.sharh: Darius killed the last of Nebuchadnezzar's sons and took over their kingdom. In the Book of Daniel, Belshazzar is killed and “Darius the Mede” receives the kingdom.

translation: In his time lived Job,
the patient, the hopeful of reward, the penitent.
187.sharh: In that age lived the prophet Job, patient under affliction, counting on God for his reward, always turning back to Him. The Quran: “We found him patient; an excellent servant, ever turning to God” (38:44).

translation: After Job, Jonah son of Amittai;
God has a book about him, read and studied.
188.sharh: After Job came Jonah son of Amittai, about whom God sent down scripture that is still read and studied: the Quran tells of him and the whale, and a sura bears his name.

translation: Jonah passed, and Isaiah rose up,
and God sent the revelation down to him.
189.sharh: When Jonah had passed on, Isaiah rose up as a prophet and God sent revelation down to him. Al-Tabari tells his story as a prophet to a king of Israel, killed in the end by his own people.

translation: It is said that al-Khidr was one of his brethren
and lived in his time.
190.sharh: Some say al-Khidr was one of Isaiah's companions and lived in his time. Al-Khidr is the mysterious servant of God whom Moses follows in the Quran (18:65); the sources place him in many different ages.

translation: Zechariah, and John the pure,
gave warning, had warnings been of any use.
191.sharh: Zechariah and his pure son John warned the Israelites, if warnings could ever have helped them. It echoes the Quran: “What use are signs and warnings to people who will not believe?” (10:101).

translation: Both were honoured with martyrdom,
and found happiness, and what happiness.
192.sharh: Both were honoured with martyrdom, and won happiness beyond measure. In the traditions John was killed for forbidding a king an unlawful marriage, and Zechariah was sawn in two inside the tree where he hid.

translation: John lived to see the son of Mary
a little child, in that ancient time.
193.sharh: John lived to see Jesus son of Mary as a little child, in that distant age. The hadith of the Night Journey calls them cousins on their mothers' side, and in the Gospels John is the elder, who later baptises Jesus.

translation: Before that, Alexander was king,
and he is the Two-Horned, as they say.
194.sharh: Before that, Alexander reigned, who, it is said, was Dhu al-Qarnayn, “the Two-Horned”, of the Quran (18:83). Many early historians made that identification, though others placed Dhu al-Qarnayn much earlier.

translation: Jesus came after the Two-Horned
by some fifty years and two hundred,
195.sharh: Jesus came about two hundred and fifty years after the Two-Horned. The figure is approximate, as “about” makes clear, and the histories disagree over it.

translation: a year less by the Byzantine reckoning,
as the well-known account records.
196.sharh: By the Byzantine reckoning the span is a year shorter, as the well-known reports have it. The Syrians and Byzantines dated events by the era of Alexander, known to the Arabs as the era of the Two-Horned.

translation: In his days were the Arsacids,
kings who raided the lands.
197.sharh: In Jesus' day the Arsacids ruled, kings who raided the lands around them. Al-Tabari counts them among the “party kings” who ruled Persia after Alexander.

translation: Ardashir cut them down with the sword,
then his son Shapur after him.
198.sharh: Ardashir cut them down with the sword and founded the Sasanian dynasty, and his son Shapur ruled after him. Ardashir overthrew the last Arsacid king in the 220s CE.

translation: Revelation ceased, and power became mere kingship,
and after the Messiah they declared idolatry openly.
199.sharh: After Christ revelation ceased: power became mere kingship, and people openly took up idolatry again. This is the “interval” between Jesus and Muhammad that the poem comes to next.

translation: He singled out the sons of Ishmael for His bounty
and made them His guests in great honour.
200.sharh: God singled out the sons of Ishmael for His favour and honoured them with great distinction, preparing the way for the Prophet who would come from among them. The poem now returns to the Arabs.

translation: They kept to Mecca and the desert,
and settled the farmlands and the fringes.
201.sharh: Ishmael's descendants kept to Mecca and the desert, and settled the farmlands and the borderlands too, spreading through Arabia and beyond.

translation: In Yemen the Tubba's appeared:
Shamir son of Ra'sh, and lawless kings.
202.sharh: In Yemen the Tubba' kings rose to power, among them Shamir son of Ra'sh, along with kings who threw off all restraint. Shamir Yur'ish is the greatest of the Tubba's in the old tales, said to have campaigned as far as Samarkand.

translation: The Byzantines took the lands of Syria,
and chose the ease of life.
203.sharh: The Byzantines took control of Syria and all its provinces and chose a life of ease and comfort there. The plural, “the Syrias”, covers all its regions.

translation: The land of Babylon came together under the Persians,
and was content with the later for the sooner.
204.sharh: The land of Babylon, that is Iraq, came together under the Persians. The second half is uncertain: one manuscript, which the editor prefers, says they were content with this world in place of the next.

translation: This is the sum of the histories of nations,
handed down by Arabs and by others.
205.sharh: Here ends the history of the ancient nations: what has gone before, he says, is a summary of their story, taken from Arab and non-Arab sources alike. A few lines of reflection follow before the coming of Islam.

translation: Every people adds and embroiders,
and seldom are things made certain.
206.sharh: Every people exaggerates its own history, and the truth of things is seldom pinned down. The poet hedges what he has told: he knows the old reports are full of embellishment.

translation: In the interval the reports went dark,
except those that poems carried abroad.
207.sharh: In the interval between Jesus and Muhammad the reports grew dim, except those that poetry carried far and wide. For the Arabs, poetry was the archive of their history.

translation: The Persians and the Byzantines have their great days,
which Islam forbids us to glorify.
208.sharh: The Persians and the Byzantines had their famous days, but Islam forbids glorifying them, since they were days of unbelief; the poet passes over their kings and moves on.

translation: The wise are content only
with the books of God and the word of the messengers.
209.sharh: Sensible people are satisfied only with God's books and the words of His messengers, not with what nations say of themselves. The section on the ancient world ends by placing revelation above report.

translation: Then the light drove away the darkness,
and all things returned to their newness.
210.sharh: Then light drove away the darkness, and everything was made new again. With this line the second part of the poem begins: the Prophet and the caliphs after him.

translation: Peoples and tribes submitted,
and there came what could not be hidden.
211.sharh: Nations and tribes submitted, and there came a truth that nothing could hide. “Peoples” and “tribes” together take in both the non-Arabs and the Arabs.

translation: There came to them the chosen one, the humble,
Muhammad, God's blessing be on him,
212.sharh: There came to them the chosen one, ever humble before God: Muhammad, God bless him. With his name the history reaches the goal it has been moving towards from the start.

translation: the noblest of God's creatures, all of them, in soul,
in birth, in origin and in descent.
213.sharh: He is the noblest of all God's creatures in soul, in birth, in origin and in lineage. A hadith traces the choosing: God chose Kinana from Ishmael's descendants, Quraysh from Kinana, Hashim from Quraysh, and Muhammad from Hashim.

translation: The noble judge him noble,
with no doubt about it, and no dispute.
214.sharh: The noble themselves judge that his nobility is beyond theirs; there is no doubt or dispute about it. Their verdict counts most, since the noble are the ones who compete for honour.

translation: He lived for years in his Mecca,
until, when he reached forty,
215.sharh: The Prophet lived in Mecca, his home town, for years, and when he reached the age of forty God sent him, as the next line says. Forty is the age of his first revelation in the biographies.

translation: God sent him to His servants:
how noble a warner and a guide.
216.sharh: God sent him to all people: how noble a warner and a guide. The Quran: “You are only a warner, and every people has a guide” (13:7).

translation: He went on calling them for thirteen years
in Mecca, before the time of the Emigration.
217.sharh: He went on calling his people in Mecca for thirteen years before the time came to emigrate to Medina: the Meccan period of his mission.

translation: Then he came to the dwelling of the Helpers,
with a band of the best of his people,
218.sharh: Then he came to the home of the Ansar, “the Helpers”, with a band of the best of his own people. The Ansar were the people of Medina, of the tribes of Aws and Khazraj, who sheltered and supported him.

translation: the first of them his companion in the cave,
the best of that righteous band,
219.sharh: First among them was his companion in the cave, Abu Bakr, the best of that righteous band. The Quran: “the second of two, when they were in the cave, and he said to his companion, ‘Do not grieve; God is with us’” (9:40).

translation: its man of truth, true in his speech,
good and gracious in his deeds.
220.sharh: He was the truthful one of that band, true in his word, good and gracious in his deeds. He was called al-Siddiq because he believed the Prophet's account of the Night Journey when others scoffed.

translation: That was in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal,
two nights after ten full ones.
221.sharh: This was in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, on the twelfth night: two after ten full ones. It is the date Ibn Ishaq gives for the Prophet's arrival in Medina.

translation: The Helpers rejoiced at the Emigrants,
and all of them preferred the abode to come.
222.sharh: The Helpers rejoiced at the arrival of the Emigrants, and all of them preferred the life to come to this one. The Quran praises the Ansar who “prefer others above themselves, though they be in need” (59:9).

translation: The tribes massed for war on him,
and truth stood firm, and falsehood vanished.
223.sharh: The tribes gathered to make war on him, at Badr, Uhud and the Trench, yet truth stood firm and falsehood vanished. The Quran: “Say: truth has come and falsehood has vanished” (17:81).

translation: He stayed in Yathrib, an emigrant,
ten years, raiding and marching out,
224.sharh: The Prophet lived ten years in Yathrib as an emigrant, raiding and marching out to war. Yathrib was Medina's name before Islam.

translation: until, when faith had prevailed,
and the idols bowed to its command,
225.sharh: Until faith had triumphed and the idols had bowed to its command: at the conquest of Mecca in 8 AH (630 CE) the idols around the Kaaba were smashed.

translation: and the Messenger delivered the message,
and the revelation and its meaning were made plain,
226.sharh: The Messenger delivered his message in full, and the Quran and its meaning were made clear. During the Farewell Pilgrimage came the verse: “Today I have perfected your religion for you” (5:3).

translation: and the abrogating and the abrogated were known,
and the era was reckoned from his Emigration,
227.sharh: People came to know which verses repealed others and which were repealed, and the Hijra became the starting point of the Muslim calendar, adopted under Umar.

translation: the One who had chosen him called, and he answered,
after He had chosen companions for him,
228.sharh: Then the One who had chosen him called him, and he answered: God took him, after choosing companions for him to carry the faith on. He died in Medina in 11 AH (632 CE).

translation: and declared them just in His clear Book,
for His servant and for people of understanding.
229.sharh: God declared those companions upright in the clear verses of His Book, for His servant and for all people of understanding to see. One manuscript adds that this is in the sura of the Gathering (59:8–9), which praises the Emigrants and the Helpers.

translation: Abu Bakr rose, whom he had appointed
to lead the people in prayer, and approved.
230.sharh: Abu Bakr took charge after the Prophet: the man the Prophet had appointed to lead the people in prayer during his last illness, a sign of his approval. The Companions argued, “He chose him for our religion; shall we not choose him for our worldly affairs?”

translation: He lived two years, and lived months,
three, and a full third more.
231.sharh: Abu Bakr held the caliphate for two years, three months and about a third of a month more. Al-Tabari gives two years, three months and some days: much the same reckoning.

translation: He died in the month of Jumada al-Akhira,
on a Tuesday, with seven nights still to run.
232.sharh: Abu Bakr died in the month of Jumada al-Akhira, 13 AH (634 CE), on a Tuesday, with seven nights of the month remaining. Al-Tabari has him die on the eve of Tuesday with eight nights remaining.

translation: In his days came the Apostasy,
and the unravelling was mended by his twisting tight.
233.sharh: In Abu Bakr's time came the Apostasy, when many Arab tribes left Islam or refused the alms tax; he fought them until they returned, and what had come undone was tied fast again. The image is of rope unravelled and twisted tight.

translation: After Abu Bakr rose Umar,
and his days shone out, those blazes of white.
234.sharh: After Abu Bakr came Umar, and his days stood out bright, like the white blaze on a horse's brow. His caliphate saw the great conquests of Persia, Syria and Egypt.

translation: The kings of Persia were shaken by him,
and the Byzantines fell on their noses.
235.sharh: The kings of Persia were shaken by him, and the Byzantines fell flat on their noses. Under Umar, Iraq, Persia, Syria and Egypt were conquered, and both great empires were broken.

translation: The Chosroes of Persia surrendered his hall,
and his horsemen were crushed.
236.sharh: The Chosroes of Persia gave up his palace hall at Ctesiphon, and his horsemen lay with their necks broken. The line plays on Faris, Persia, fursan, horsemen, and mafrusa, crushed.

translation: The Byzantines withdrew from Syria
and turned their backs in fear of Islam.
237.sharh: The Byzantines withdrew from Syria and fled for fear of Islam, after their defeat at the Yarmuk in 15 AH (636 CE). Heraclius is said to have bidden Syria a farewell “with no meeting after it”.

translation: The regions submitted to al-Faruq,
and opened wide for him after narrowness.
238.sharh: The lands submitted to al-Faruq, and Islam's domain, once narrow, grew wide in his time, stretching from Persia to Egypt.

translation: God granted him martyrdom,
an end that showed his blessedness.
239.sharh: God granted Umar martyrdom: he was stabbed by Abu Lu'lu'a while leading the dawn prayer in 23 AH (644 CE), an end that showed his blessedness. He used to pray for martyrdom in the Prophet's city, and was granted it.

translation: That was after ten years
and half a year: and what a half.
240.sharh: That came after ten years and half a year of his rule, “and what a half it was”, for all that happened in it. Al-Tabari gives Umar the same span.

translation: Uthman ibn Affan, the approved, took the charge
for twelve years, then passed away,
241.sharh: Uthman ibn Affan, the well-pleasing, then held the caliphate for twelve years before he passed away: from the beginning of 24 AH to 35 AH (644–656 CE).

translation: a martyr on the road of truth;
the byways did not turn him from it.
242.sharh: Uthman died a martyr on the road of truth, never drawn off it by the little byways of faction and temptation. He was killed in his house in Medina, refusing to let anyone fight for him.

translation: The charge was given to Ali,
the Hashimite, the excellent, the pure.
243.sharh: Then the charge was entrusted to Ali, of the house of Hashim, excellent and pure, who received the oath in Medina after Uthman's murder in 35 AH (656 CE). He was the Prophet's cousin and the husband of his daughter Fatima.

translation: He held the charge for four years
and nine months, all told.
244.sharh: Ali held the caliphate for four years and nine full months, the length al-Tabari gives for his rule, much of it spent in civil war.

translation: Then he passed, a martyr, praised;
he lived praiseworthy, and passed away mourned.
245.sharh: Then Ali died a martyr, praised: he lived a praiseworthy life and was mourned when he was gone. He was struck down in Kufa by Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam in Ramadan 40 AH (661 CE).

translation: This was in the year forty
that had passed of the count of the years.
246.sharh: This was in the year forty, counting the years since the Hijra. With it ends the age of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs.

translation: The charge passed from Medina,
and what Safina reported proved true
247.sharh: The seat of power left Medina for good, and what Safina had reported from the Prophet came true. Ali had already moved to Kufa; under Mu'awiya, Damascus became the capital.

translation: from the Prophet, about those who would rule the community,
the kings and the imams.
248.sharh: Safina's report from the Prophet was about who would rule the community: rightly guided leaders for thirty years, then kings. The four caliphs together reigned about thirty years, so the hadith came true.

translation: Then Mu'awiya took charge of them,
and lived ten years after ten gone by,
249.sharh: Then Mu'awiya took charge of the community and ruled for twenty years, ten after ten. With him the Umayyad dynasty began, ruling from Damascus.

translation: until, when he had given them twenty full,
he died, in the year sixty of the era.
250.sharh: When he had given them twenty full years of rule, he died, in the year sixty of the Hijra calendar (680 CE). He had named his son Yazid as heir, the first to make the caliphate hereditary.

translation: His son Yazid seized the rule,
neither firm of judgement nor rightly guided.
251.sharh: Mu'awiya's son Yazid took power, a man neither firm in judgement nor rightly guided. The poet condemns him plainly for the bloodshed of his reign.

translation: Al-Husayn was killed in his time;
I seek refuge with the Merciful from his betrayal.
252.sharh: In Yazid's time al-Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed at Karbala in 61 AH (680 CE); the poet seeks refuge in God from the betrayal that left him to die.

translation: He lived only three years
and months after the burden of that going-out.
253.sharh: Yazid ruled only three years and some months, dying in 64 AH (683 CE). The end of the line is obscure; one manuscript reads it differently, and it may refer to al-Husayn's setting out for Iraq.

translation: Then his son, little Mu'awiya, the weakened,
a man of known faith and sense.
254.sharh: Next came Yazid's son Mu'awiya, called the weak, though known for his piety and good sense. This line and the next two are not in the diwan's text; the editor notes that Ibn Zafar quotes them as Ali ibn al-Jahm's in his Sulwan al-Muta'.

translation: He lasted a month, then half a month more,
and death came to him while his rule stood strong.
255.sharh: He lasted a month and a half, and death came to him while his rule was still unchallenged. The reports of his reign vary from forty days to three months.

translation: He left the people without a covenant,
out of caution, and the grace of renunciation.
256.sharh: He left the people without naming a successor, out of caution and an unusual indifference to power. In the reports he refused to carry its burden in life and in death, and left the choice to the people.

translation: The charge was entrusted to Marwan
after Yazid, an old man near his end.
257.sharh: Power then passed to Marwan ibn al-Hakam, an old man near the end of his life. He received the oath at al-Jabiya in 64 AH (684 CE), and the Umayyad throne passed to his branch of the family.

translation: He killed al-Dahhak in Dhu al-Qa'da
at Rahit, then won over his army.
258.sharh: Marwan killed al-Dahhak ibn Qays, who had declared for Ibn al-Zubayr in Syria, at Marj Rahit, and won over his troops. The poet puts it in Dhu al-Qa'da; the battle was fought late in 64 AH (684 CE).

translation: He lived only ten months;
nothing goes beyond its measure.
259.sharh: Marwan lived only ten months as caliph and died in 65 AH (685 CE), for nothing can go beyond its appointed measure. The second half is a maxim closing his story.

translation: Ibn al-Zubayr went on after him
for nine years, sparing no effort,
260.sharh: Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr held out for nine years after Yazid, sparing no effort, recognised as caliph in Mecca and the Hijaz, and for a time in Iraq.

translation: holding to the sacred Kaaba,
holding out against the rulers of Syria,
261.sharh: He took refuge in the sacred Kaaba and held out against the Umayyad rulers in Syria, refusing them his allegiance; he was known as “the one who sought refuge in the House”.

translation: until al-Hajjaj saw to his killing,
after the wide passes had grown narrow for him.
262.sharh: In the end al-Hajjaj, Abd al-Malik's general, killed him, after besieging him in Mecca until even the wide mountain passes were closed to him. He died in 73 AH (692 CE).

translation: Then came the wrecking of the guarded Kaaba,
and the Battle of the Harra at Medina.
263.sharh: Those years of strife saw the Kaaba itself wrecked, struck by catapults during the sieges of Ibn al-Zubayr, and the Battle of the Harra in 63 AH (683 CE), when Yazid's army sacked Medina.

translation: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan rose,
rousing for war, never drowsy,
264.sharh: After Marwan his son Abd al-Malik took up the rule, rousing men to war and never caught napping: at the time Ibn al-Zubayr was recognised as caliph across most of the empire.

translation: until, when the horizons bowed to him,
and Iraq was emptied of Mus'ab,
265.sharh: Until the far regions all submitted to him, and Iraq was emptied of Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr, whom Abd al-Malik defeated and killed at Dayr al-Jathaliq in 72 AH (691 CE).

translation: and the Sacred City of his brother,
and all people feared his might,
266.sharh: Mecca, the sacred city, was emptied of his brother Abd Allah, and all people feared Abd al-Malik's might: by 73 AH (692 CE) the whole empire was his.

translation: he died, having lived thirteen years
and four months in command.
267.sharh: Abd al-Malik died after thirteen years and four months in power. The poet counts his reign from the death of Ibn al-Zubayr, when everyone accepted him, not from his accession in 65 AH; he died in 86 AH (705 CE).

translation: His son al-Walid ruled the people,
with wealth and armies at his side,
268.sharh: Abd al-Malik's son al-Walid ruled next, with wealth and armies at his command. Under him Muslim armies took Spain, Transoxiana and Sind, and he built the Great Mosque of Damascus.

translation: seven years, and after them eight
full months, complete.
269.sharh: Al-Walid reigned seven years and eight full months, the poem says. One manuscript reads “nine years”, closer to the historians, who give him nine years and some months.

translation: Then Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik,
chosen for the succession, and not passed over.
270.sharh: Then came Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik, chosen by his father as heir after al-Walid and never set aside, although al-Walid tried to replace him with his own son.

translation: He lived two years and two-thirds of a year,
then came to Dabiq with his train trailing.
271.sharh: Sulayman ruled two years and two-thirds of a year, then came to Dabiq, at ease and in state, to direct the siege of Constantinople, and died there in 99 AH (717 CE).

translation: He died, and Umar took over the rule,
with a conduct praised among all conducts.
272.sharh: Sulayman died, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, whom he had named, took power and ruled in a way praised above all others; he is often counted a fifth Rightly Guided Caliph.

translation: He lived two years and half a year
at Dayr Sim'an, less some days.
273.sharh: Umar ruled two and a half years, less a few days, and died at Dayr Sim'an, near Ma'arrat al-Nu'man, in 101 AH (720 CE), where he was buried.

translation: Then Yazid took charge of them;
God does whatever He wills.
274.sharh: Then Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik took charge of them, and God does whatever He wills. The second half quotes the Quran (85:16); after the just Umar, it sounds like resignation.

translation: He was of the sons of Abd al-Malik,
the third of them in his shared succession.
275.sharh: Yazid was the third of Abd al-Malik's sons to rule, after al-Walid and Sulayman, under a succession shared among them; Sulayman had named Umar first and Yazid after him.

translation: He lived two years on top of two,
