and some months, with his eye at peace.
276.sharh: Yazid ruled four years and some months, content and untroubled. He was famous for his love of singing girls; when his favourite, Hababa, died, he died of grief soon after, in 105 AH (724 CE).

translation: Then after him came Hisham,
his brother, and his days stretched long.
277.sharh: Yazid was followed by his brother Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, whose reign was long: he was the last strong ruler of the Umayyad house.

translation: He went on ruling twenty years,
but for five months remaining.
278.sharh: Hisham ruled for twenty years less five months, close to the figure the historians give; he governed from al-Rusafa in the Syrian desert.

translation: Then al-Walid son of Yazid, the heedless:
brave lions took turns at him
279.sharh: Then came al-Walid son of Yazid, the heedless, and fierce lions took turns at him until he fell. He was notorious for his pleasures and was himself a poet.

translation: after two months and after a year
and after twenty days.
280.sharh: That came after a year, two months and twenty days of his reign: he was killed in 126 AH (744 CE). The poem counts his reign to the day, like a chronicle.

translation: His cousin made war on him,
condemning his conduct, so he claimed.
281.sharh: His cousin Yazid ibn al-Walid made war on him, condemning his conduct, or so he claimed. It was the first open war within the house of Marwan.

translation: Al-Walid was killed at al-Bakhra'
after he had dealt his enemies heavy blows.
282.sharh: Al-Walid was killed at the fortress of al-Bakhra' near Palmyra after inflicting heavy losses on his enemies. In the reports he took up a copy of the Quran at the end and said, “A day like Uthman's day.”

translation: Then Yazid son of al-Walid, the Reducer:
the doom that seizes seized him.
283.sharh: Next came Yazid ibn al-Walid, called al-Naqis, “the Reducer”, for cutting the soldiers' pay, and death, which takes people by surprise, seized him quickly.

translation: He lived only six months
until the fates removed him, suddenly.
284.sharh: Yazid lived only six months as caliph before death swept him away without warning, in the same year he came to power, 126 AH (744 CE).

translation: They all swore allegiance to Marwan,
and he was a strong fortress for them.
285.sharh: Then everyone swore allegiance to Marwan ibn Muhammad, the last Umayyad caliph, who stood like a strong fortress for them. He was nicknamed “the Donkey” for his endurance in war.

translation: He went on ruling them five full years
and eight months.
286.sharh: Marwan ruled them for five full years and eight months, until the Abbasids defeated him on the river Zab and he was killed in Egypt in 132 AH (750 CE).

translation: Until God, Master of blessing, brought
the truth from Him, in kindness and in mercy.
287.sharh: Until God, the Master of blessings, brought the truth, out of kindness and mercy: the coming of the Abbasids. Ali ibn al-Jahm was an Abbasid court poet, and presents their rise as right restored.

translation: He chose for the people Abu al-Abbas,
from the bravest of men, the best of men,
288.sharh: God chose for the people Abu al-Abbas, first of the Abbasid caliphs, from the bravest and best of mankind. He received the oath of allegiance in Kufa in 132 AH (749 CE).

translation: the Prophet's family, of the sons of al-Abbas,
imams, excellent and wise.
289.sharh: He was of the Prophet's family, the house of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle: leaders, excellent and wise. The Abbasids based their claim to the caliphate on that kinship.

translation: The blade of kingship went back in its sheath,
and the right returned to its owners.
290.sharh: The blade of kingship went back into its scabbard, and the right returned to those who owned it: in the poet's eyes, the Prophet's own clan.

translation: Then he climbed the pulpit on Friday
in the mosque of Kufa, shedding tears.
291.sharh: Abu al-Abbas then climbed the pulpit of the mosque of Kufa on a Friday, the day of his accession, shedding tears, and gave the speech that proclaimed the new dynasty.

translation: He stood for the faith as one like him would stand,
with his blessed judgement, as his deeds deserved.
292.sharh: He stood up for the faith as only a man like him could, with his auspicious judgement, as his deeds required. The line is general praise for the dynasty's first caliph.

translation: He died after four full years
and seven months over and above.
293.sharh: Abu al-Abbas died after four full years and seven months more, at al-Anbar in 136 AH (754 CE).

translation: Al-Mansur took up the caliphate,
and by his resolve all things came into order.
294.sharh: Al-Mansur, Abu al-Abbas's brother, then took the caliphate, and with his resolve everything fell into order. He was the founder of Baghdad and the real architect of Abbasid power.

translation: He lived twenty-two years,
guarding the bounds of the realm and destroying traitors,
295.sharh: Al-Mansur ruled for twenty-two years, guarding the sanctuary of the throne and wiping out traitors: he crushed his uncle Abd Allah ibn Ali, had Abu Muslim killed and put down the revolt of al-Nafs al-Zakiyya.

translation: until he died, in pilgrim's garb, at Mecca,
and al-Mahdi inherited his kingdom from him.
296.sharh: Until al-Mansur died in the pilgrim's state of consecration near Mecca, in 158 AH (775 CE), and his son al-Mahdi inherited his throne. He died at Bi'r Maymun, just short of the city.

translation: He lived ten years and a month
and half a month, then visited the grave.
297.sharh: Al-Mahdi ruled ten years, a month and half a month, and then “visited the grave”: he died in 169 AH (785 CE). The phrase is a gentle way of saying he died.

translation: He left al-Hadi, Musa, as caliph after him,
having already made him his heir.
298.sharh: Al-Mahdi was succeeded by his son Musa al-Hadi, whom he had already named heir, so power passed to him without dispute.

translation: Musa lived a year and two months,
less one day, or two.
299.sharh: Musa ruled a year and two months, less a day or two, and died in 170 AH (786 CE). The poet reckons as precisely as a chronicler.

translation: Al-Rashid took up the caliphate,
the king, well guarded, fortunate.
300.sharh: Then Harun al-Rashid took the caliphate, a well-defended and fortunate king. Under him the Abbasid empire reached the height of its power and wealth.

translation: He lived twenty, and filled their count,
and lived two years, and a year after,
301.sharh: Al-Rashid ruled twenty full years, then two more and one after that: twenty-three in all, from 170 to 193 AH (786–809 CE), as the historians reckon.

translation: and half a month; then his end came to him
at Tus, on a Saturday, and the mountain fell.
302.sharh: And half a month more; then his end came at Tus, on a Saturday, and a mountain fell. He had marched east to put down the rebel Rafi' ibn al-Layth and died on the way.

translation: They swore allegiance to Muhammad al-Amin,
and broke their pledge, all of them,
303.sharh: People swore allegiance to Muhammad al-Amin, al-Rashid's son, then broke their oath to a man when war broke out between him and his brother al-Ma'mun. Al-Rashid had named al-Amin heir, with al-Ma'mun after him.

translation: but for a few, and the few are more praiseworthy;
death is an appointment for all people.
304.sharh: Except for a few who stayed loyal, and the few are the more praiseworthy; death is everyone's appointment. The maxim hints that betrayal gains nothing in the end.

translation: They promised him safety, then fought him:
that was not what his father pledged them to.
305.sharh: They gave al-Amin a promise of safety, then fought him: this was not the pact his father had made them swear. He was killed in 198 AH (813 CE) after surrendering under a guarantee of safe conduct.

translation: He lived only four years and some months,
till they passed his head about, soiled with dust.
306.sharh: Al-Amin lasted only four years and some months, until his head, smeared with dust, was passed from hand to hand and sent to his brother al-Ma'mun in Khurasan.

translation: They swore allegiance to al-Ma'mun, Abd Allah,
and swore it to a man awake, not heedless.
307.sharh: Then people swore allegiance to al-Ma'mun, Abd Allah son of al-Rashid: a man wide awake, never careless. He was the most learned of the Abbasid caliphs, and Baghdad's great age of translation flourished under him.

translation: He gave them the span of al-Mansur's caliphate,
in the count of years and of months.
308.sharh: Al-Ma'mun gave them a caliphate as long as al-Mansur's, in years and in months: about twenty-two years, if counted from when he renounced his brother al-Amin in 196 AH (812 CE).

translation: Then he went against the Byzantines and died raiding;
al-Badhandun was his farthest halt.
309.sharh: Then al-Ma'mun invaded Byzantine territory and died on campaign; al-Badhandun was the farthest place he reached. He was carried to Tarsus and buried there in 218 AH (833 CE).

translation: The command was given to Abu Ishaq,
and he swooped like a falcon on Iraq,
310.sharh: Then the command passed to Abu Ishaq, al-Ma'mun's brother, who was with him on campaign; he swooped on Iraq like a falcon to secure his throne before anyone could contest it.

translation: clinging to God, not heedless,
and he strengthened the rule with fine judgement.
311.sharh: He held fast to God, as his title al-Mu'tasim bi-llah, “the one who clings to God”, declares, never careless, and strengthened the state with his excellent judgement. The opening words are both a description and his regnal title.

translation: He ruled them eight years,
and as many months besides,
312.sharh: Al-Mu'tasim ruled them for eight years and as many months, close to the historians' figure, with some days more, which the next line adds.

translation: and some twenty days,
and five that brought him close to death.
313.sharh: And about twenty-five days, which brought him to his death in 227 AH (842 CE). Each Abbasid reign in the poem is counted to the month, sometimes to the day.

translation: He died in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal,
his age fifty, not yet complete.
314.sharh: Al-Mu'tasim died in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, 227 AH (842 CE), not yet fifty years old. The reports put his birth around 180 AH (796 CE).

translation: After him they swore allegiance to al-Wathiq,
and that was by the decree that went before.
315.sharh: After al-Mu'tasim, people swore allegiance to his son al-Wathiq, as God had decreed beforehand: each succession, for the poet, is written in advance.

translation: He went on in plenty and in strength
five years and nine months,
316.sharh: Al-Wathiq lived in ease and security for five years and nine months. A lover of literature and music, he also kept up the inquisition over the createdness of the Quran.

translation: and added five days to them,
counted out, then disappeared in his grave.
317.sharh: And five more days, counted out; then he vanished into his grave. He died at Samarra in 232 AH (847 CE).

translation: The people swore allegiance to the imam Ja'far,
God's deputy, the bright-browed, the radiant,
318.sharh: People then swore allegiance to the imam Ja'far, al-Mutawakkil, God's deputy, radiant and shining. Al-Mutawakkil was the caliph Ali ibn al-Jahm served and praised most, though he later fell from favour, was jailed and was exiled.

translation: after two hundred and thirty years,
and after two years, less some days,
319.sharh: This was two hundred and thirty years after the Hijra, and two more less a few days: at the very end of 232 AH (847 CE), after his brother al-Wathiq's death.

translation: gone by since the Hijra, by the reckoning
of the Arabs, exact and correct,
320.sharh: Years since the Hijra, that is, by the Arab lunar reckoning, precise and correct, not by the Byzantine or Persian calendars the poem used for the nations before Islam.

translation: with six nights left of Dhu al-Hijja,
and he made the road and the highway plain.
321.sharh: The oath was taken with six nights of Dhu al-Hijja left, and al-Mutawakkil made the road plain. He ended the inquisition over the createdness of the Quran, which is why the poet praises him for clearing the way.

translation: He stood among the people as their caliph,
a caliphate lofty and noble.
322.sharh: He stood among the people as their caliph, with a caliphate lofty and noble. One manuscript praises instead his lofty and noble character.

translation: Through him God has calmed the borders,
and you see no dissent in his realm.
323.sharh: Through him God calmed the borderlands, and no revolt or dissent is to be seen in his realm. The rhyme plays on khilafa, caliphate, and khilaf, dissent.

translation: He reigned ten years, then five more
years after, and made its glory plain.
324.sharh: Al-Mutawakkil reigned ten years and then five more, about fifteen in all, and made the caliphate's glory plain to see.

translation: Then the men of Farghana saw to his killing,
helped by a gang of pharaohs,
325.sharh: Then the men of Farghana, Turkish guards from Central Asia, killed him, helped by a band of pharaohs, tyrants in their own right. The rhyme pairs Faraghina with fara'ina, pharaohs; the reports say his son al-Muntasir knew of the plot.

translation: with four nights of Shawwal gone,
and the kingdom became disorder's brother.
326.sharh: He was killed with four nights of Shawwal gone, in 247 AH (861 CE), and from then on the state was a brother to disorder. Historians date the Turkish generals' grip on the caliphate from his murder.

translation: After him they swore allegiance to al-Muntasir,
and the winner among them found he had lost.
327.sharh: Then they swore allegiance to his son al-Muntasir, and those who thought they had won found they had lost: al-Muntasir himself did not live to enjoy his throne.

translation: He lived in power six months;
he put them out of his realm and out of the camp.
328.sharh: Al-Muntasir held power for six months, in which he forced his brothers al-Mu'tazz and al-Mu'ayyad out of the succession and out of “the camp”, that is Samarra, the capital of the time.

translation: Then his death came on him suddenly:
glory to Him whose vengeance hastens.
329.sharh: Then death came on him suddenly: glory to God, whose vengeance comes swiftly. The poet treats his death as quick punishment for his father's murder; some reports say he was poisoned.

translation: God chose an imam for them,
through whom God supports Islam.
330.sharh: God chose an imam for them, through whom He strengthens Islam: al-Musta'in, named in the next line, the caliph reigning when the poem was finished.

translation: With one accord they swore allegiance to Ahmad,
al-Musta'in, who seeks the help of the one God.
331.sharh: With their consent they swore allegiance to Ahmad al-Musta'in, “he who seeks help from God”, the One. As with al-Mu'tasim, the line uses the caliph's title as a description too.

translation: He was the twelfth of its rulers,
of the house of Abbas, and of its defenders.
332.sharh: Al-Musta'in was the twelfth of the Abbasid rulers and defenders of the caliphate, counting from Abu al-Abbas.

translation: We are now in a blessed caliphate,
free of harm and of rivals.
333.sharh: “We live now under a blessed caliphate, free of harm and of any rival sharing its power.” The history ends in the poet's own day: Ali ibn al-Jahm died in 249 AH (863 CE), a year after al-Musta'in's accession.

translation: Praise be to God for His bounty:
all of this is of His decrees.
334.sharh: He ends with praise of God for His blessings: everything the poem has told, every nation and every king, has unfolded by God's decree. The closing praise answers the opening one.

translation: Then peace, first and last,
on the Prophet, inwardly and outwardly.
335.sharh: Finally he sends peace on the Prophet, first and last, inwardly and outwardly, as he did at the start. The line repeats the poem's second line almost word for word, with “peace” in place of “blessings”.

1.1.3.head: المُعيد
1.1.3.meaning: Al-Mu'id: the One who brings creation back after death; with al-Mubdi', “the One who begins”, a pair of divine names.

2.1.2.head: الصَّلاة
2.1.2.meaning: Salat: here the prayer of blessing on the Prophet, not the ritual prayer.

4.2.4.head: هَيئات
4.2.4.meaning: Hay'at: bearings; men of gravity and standing.

5.1.4.head: الآثار
5.1.4.meaning: Athar: reports handed down about earlier generations.

6.2.2.head: التَّنزيل
6.2.2.meaning: Tanzil: “what was sent down”, the Quran.

6.2.3.head: التَّأويل
6.2.3.meaning: Ta'wil: the interpretation of the Quran.

8.1.3.head: آدَم
8.1.3.meaning: Adam: the first man, father of humankind.

8.2.4.head: حَوّاء
8.2.4.meaning: Hawwa': Eve, Adam's wife and the mother of humankind.

9.1.3-4.meaning: “The day of gathering”: Friday, the day of the congregational prayer.

10.1.3.head: الجِنان
10.1.3.meaning: Jinan: gardens; here the Garden where Adam was first placed.

11.1.2.head: إِبليس
11.1.2.meaning: Iblis: Satan, who refused to bow down to Adam.

12.1.1.head: دَلّى
12.1.1.meaning: Dallahuma: “let them down” like a bucket into a well; lured them into a fall.

13.2.5.meaning: Wasim: the mountain in India where, al-Tabari reports from the people of the Torah, Adam was sent down.

14.2.4.head: المَنّان
14.2.4.meaning: Al-Mannan: the Bountiful, a name of God.

16.2.4-5.meaning: “A toiling toil”: the hardest labour; the repetition intensifies it.

18.2.3-4.meaning: “Words from his Lord”: most commentators take them to be “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we shall be among the lost” (7:23).

19.2.2.head: تَوّاب
19.2.2.meaning: Tawwab: “ever-relenting”, a name of God: He turns to those who repent.

22.1.4.head: قايِن
22.1.4.meaning: Qayin: Cain, Adam's firstborn, who killed his brother; Arabic sources also call him Qabil.

28.1.2.meaning: Istafazza: unsettled her and lured her away.

30.1.4.head: شيث
30.1.4.meaning: Shith: Seth, Adam's son born after Abel's death, ancestor of Noah.

31.2.4.head: مِئَة
31.2.4.meaning: Miyya: mi'a, “hundred”, its hamza softened, as the meter requires.

32.1.5.meaning: Wasiyya: a testament; here the charge of leadership Adam passes to Seth.

37.1.2.head: أَنوش
37.1.2.meaning: Anush: Enosh, son of Seth; al-Tabari also calls him Yanish.

41.1.4.head: يَرد
41.1.4.meaning: Yard: Jared, son of Mahalalel and father of Enoch; also Yarid (line 47).

41.2.1.head: أَخنوخ
41.2.1.meaning: Akhnukh: Enoch, identified with the prophet Idris.

42.1.4.head: توبيل
42.1.4.meaning: Tubil: Tubal, of Cain's line; al-Tabari, from the Torah, says he made the first instruments of music.

42.2.3.head: الضِّلّيل
42.2.3.meaning: Dillil: one who strays far and again and again.

45.1.5.head: عالَم
45.1.5.meaning: Alam: a world; here a great multitude.

48.2.1.head: إِدريس
48.2.1.meaning: Idris: a prophet named in the Quran, identified with Enoch, great-grandfather of Noah.

49.1.2.head: خَنوخ
49.1.2.meaning: Khanukh: Enoch, Idris's name in the Torah.

54.1.2.head: مَتّوشَلَخ
54.1.2.meaning: Mattushalakh: Methuselah, son of Enoch and grandfather of Noah.

56.1.3.head: لَمك
56.1.3.meaning: Lamk: Lamech, son of Methuselah and father of Noah.

63.1.3-4.meaning: “The prayer of ruin”: a prayer for their destruction.

67.1.5.head: آب
67.1.5.meaning: Ab: the Syriac month that corresponds to August.

68.1.4.meaning: Ma'ma'a: din and turmoil; here the onset of the Flood.

71.2.5.head: يافِث
71.2.5.meaning: Yafith: Japheth, Noah's youngest son in this account.

73.2.1.head: يَأجوج
73.2.1.meaning: Ya'juj: Gog, named in the Quran with Magog.

74.2.1.head: أَرفَخشَذ
74.2.1.meaning: Arfakhshadh: Arpachshad, son of Shem, an ancestor of Abraham.

75.1.5.head: عاد
75.1.5.meaning: Ad: an ancient Arab people, to whom the prophet Hud was sent.

76.2.4.head: جَديس
76.2.4.meaning: Jadis: an extinct Arab tribe of al-Yamama.

76.2.5.head: طَسَم
76.2.5.meaning: Tasm: an extinct Arab tribe of al-Yamama, neighbour and enemy of Jadis.

77.1.4.head: هود
77.1.4.meaning: Hud: the prophet sent to Ad; a sura of the Quran bears his name.

79.1.4.head: أَعَزَّ
79.1.4.meaning: A'izza: make scarce; that is, withhold.

81.2.3.head: مَكَّة
81.2.3.meaning: Mecca: the sacred city; in al-Tabari, people in trouble went to pray at its sanctuary even then.

82.2.2-4.meaning: Luqman ibn Ad: chief of Ad in the old tales, proverbial for his long life.

83.2.4.head: النُّسور
83.2.4.meaning: Nusur: vultures; Luqman's seven vultures, a byword for long life.

85.1.2.head: ثَمود
85.1.2.meaning: Thamud: an ancient Arab people, to whom the prophet Salih was sent.

85.2.2.head: الحِجر
85.2.2.meaning: Al-Hijr: the land of Thamud in the northern Hijaz, today Mada'in Salih.

86.1.4.head: صالِح
86.1.4.meaning: Salih: the prophet sent to Thamud.

90.2.4.head: فَصيل
90.2.4.meaning: Fasil: a camel's foal, newly weaned.

91.1.1.head: عَقَرَ
91.1.1.meaning: Aqaru: hamstrung, crippled by cutting the legs, then slaughtered.

91.2.2-3.meaning: “The shout of extinction”: the blast that destroyed Thamud.

93.1.4.head: إِبراهيم
93.1.4.meaning: Ibrahim: Abraham, God's Friend, father of Ishmael and Isaac.

94.1.4.head: التَّوحيد
94.1.4.meaning: Tawhid: belief in the oneness of God.

95.1.2.head: الشَّرائِع
95.1.2.meaning: Shara'i': laws, the ordinances of religion.

99.1.2.head: النُّمرود
99.1.2.meaning: Al-Namrud: Nimrod, the tyrant king of Abraham's time in the traditions.

101.1.3.head: إِسماعيل
101.1.3.meaning: Isma'il: Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, ancestor of the northern Arabs.

101.2.4.head: الخَليل
101.2.4.meaning: Al-Khalil: “the Friend”, Abraham's title in the Quran (4:125).

102.1.4.meaning: Sara: Sarah, Abraham's first wife and mother of Isaac.

103.2.1-3.meaning: “God has heard”: the meaning of the Hebrew name Ishmael.

104.1.3-4.meaning: “The secure city”: Mecca, so called in the Quran (95:3).

104.2.4.head: الحَجون
104.2.4.meaning: Al-Hajun: a hill on the upper side of Mecca, by the town's old cemetery.

105.1.4.head: جِبريل
105.1.4.meaning: Jibril: Gabriel, the angel of revelation.

107.1.4.head: جُمجُم
107.1.4.meaning: Jumjum: so the edition's base text, as the reciter voices it, with no sense here; the editor reads zamzam, “abundant water”, the name of the well at Mecca.

107.2.4-5.meaning: Anhura ma: “rivers of water”, the word for water shortened for the rhyme.

110.1.2.head: جُرهُم
110.1.2.meaning: Jurhum: an ancient Arab tribe from the south who settled in Mecca; Ishmael married among them.

111.2.1.head: خُؤولَة
111.2.1.meaning: Khu'ula: kinship through the mother; Jurhum were the maternal uncles of Ishmael's sons.

112.1.3-4.meaning: “An age of ages”: a very long time.

114.1.4.meaning: Kinana: an Arab tribe descended from Ishmael; Quraysh is one of its branches.

115.2.4.head: إِلياس
115.2.4.meaning: Ilyas: Ilyas son of Mudar, an ancestor of the Prophet and of Quraysh.

117.1.5.head: قُصَيّ
117.1.5.meaning: Qusayy: Qusayy ibn Kilab, the chief who made Quraysh masters of Mecca; an ancestor of the Prophet.

118.1.4.head: المَقام
118.1.4.meaning: Al-Maqam: the Station of Abraham, the stone he stood on while building the Kaaba.

118.2.2.head: المَشعَر
118.2.2.meaning: Al-Mash'ar: the pilgrimage sites, al-Mash'ar al-Haram at Muzdalifa above all.

119.1.1-4.meaning: “The bow went to its carver”: the task fell to the one who knows how to do it.

122.1.4.head: إِسحاق
122.1.4.meaning: Ishaq: Isaac, son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob.

124.2.2.head: الصّادِق
124.2.2.meaning: Al-Sadiq: “the truthful”; the Quran calls Ishmael “true to his promise” (19:54).

127.1.4.head: يَعقوب
127.1.4.meaning: Ya'qub: Jacob, son of Isaac, also called Israel, father of the twelve tribes.

130.2.2.head: يوسُف
130.2.2.meaning: Yusuf: Joseph, son of Jacob; the twelfth sura of the Quran bears his name.

133.2.4.head: الشَّآم
133.2.4.meaning: Al-Sha'am: Syria in the wide sense, including Palestine.

135.2.2-5.meaning: “Fulfilled his need of life”: lived as long as he wished.

138.1.2.head: فِرعَون
138.1.2.meaning: Fir'awn: Pharaoh, the title of the kings of ancient Egypt.

139.1.4.meaning: Musa: Moses, son of Imran, the prophet of the children of Israel.

145.1.3.head: التّيه
145.1.3.meaning: Al-Tih: “the wandering”, the wilderness where the Israelites wandered forty years.

146.1.2-4.meaning: Harun ibn Imran: Aaron, brother of Moses.

148.1.3-5.meaning: Yusha' ibn Nun: Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor.

149.1.3.head: الأُردُنّ
149.1.3.meaning: Urdun: the river Jordan, called a sea for its water.

150.1.4.meaning: Ariha: Jericho, the first city Joshua took.

153.1.3-4.meaning: Bani Isra'il: the children of Israel, descendants of Jacob, whose other name was Israel.

154.2.2.head: الأَسباط
154.2.2.meaning: Asbat: the twelve tribes of Israel.

155.1.3.head: حِزقائيل
155.1.3.meaning: Hizqil: Ezekiel, called the son of the old woman.

156.2.2.head: بَعل
156.2.2.meaning: Ba'l: Baal, the idol the Israelites worshipped in Elijah's time.

157.1.2-4.meaning: Ilyas ibn Yasin: Elijah, a prophet of Aaron's line.

162.1.3-5.meaning: Ibn al-Khutub al-Yasa': Elisha son of Akhtub, Elijah's successor.

163.1.2.head: التّابوت
163.1.2.meaning: Al-Tabut: the Ark of the Covenant.

163.2.2.meaning: Ali: Eli, the priest and head of Israel (Ayli in al-Tabari); not the caliph Ali.

165.1.3.head: سَمويل
165.1.3.meaning: Samwil: Samuel, the prophet who made Saul king.

168.1.4.head: طالوت
168.1.4.meaning: Talut: Saul, the first king of Israel.

169.1.2.head: داوُد
169.1.2.meaning: Dawud: David, prophet and king, who killed Goliath.

173.2.4.head: مِخلاة
173.2.4.meaning: Mikhlat: a feed bag; here David's shepherd's pouch.

175.2.5.head: مَظِنَّة
175.2.5.meaning: Mazinna: the place where something is expected to be found.

178.1.4-5.meaning: Bayt al-Maqdis: “the Holy House”, the Temple in Jerusalem, and the city itself.

179.1.3.meaning: Sulayman: Solomon, son of David, prophet and king.

185.1.2.head: الرَّملَة
185.1.2.meaning: Al-Ramla: a town in Palestine, founded under the Umayyads.

187.1.4.head: أَيّوب
187.1.4.meaning: Ayyub: Job, proverbial for his patience.

188.1.3-5.meaning: Yunus ibn Matta: Jonah son of Amittai, swallowed by the whale.

190.1.3.head: الخِضر
190.1.3.meaning: Al-Khidr: “the Green One”, the servant of God whom Moses meets in the Quran.

194.2.2-3.meaning: Dhu al-Qarnayn: “the Two-Horned”, a righteous king in the Quran who built a wall against Gog and Magog.

197.1.4.head: الأَشغانيّون
197.1.4.meaning: Al-Ashghanun: the Arsacids, the Parthian kings of Persia.

198.1.3.head: أَردَشير
198.1.3.meaning: Ardashir: Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian dynasty.

202.1.3.meaning: Tababi'a: the Tubba's, kings of Himyar in Yemen.

202.2.1-3.meaning: Shamir ibn Ra'sh: Shamir Yur'ish, a Himyarite king.

204.1.4.head: بابِل
204.1.4.meaning: Babil: Babylon; its land is Iraq.

207.1.3.head: الفَترَة
207.1.3.meaning: Al-Fatra: the interval between two prophets; here between Jesus and Muhammad.

212.1.3.head: الأَوّاه
212.1.3.meaning: Awwah: one who sighs often in awe of God; tender-hearted.

216.2.1-2.meaning: “How noble is he”: an exclamatory form.

217.2.4.meaning: Al-Hijra: the Emigration of the Prophet from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

218.1.4.head: الأَنصار
218.1.4.meaning: Al-Ansar: “the Helpers”, the Muslims of Medina.

219.1.2-4.meaning: “His companion in the cave”: Abu Bakr, who hid with the Prophet in the cave of Thawr.

221.1.4-5.meaning: Rabi' al-Awwal: the third month of the Islamic year.

222.1.3.head: المُهاجِرَة
222.1.3.meaning: Al-Muhajira: the Emigrants who left Mecca for Medina.

224.1.4.head: يَثرِب
224.1.4.meaning: Yathrib: the old name of Medina.

227.1.2-3.meaning: Al-nasikh wa-l-mansukh: the abrogating and the abrogated verses of the Quran.

229.1.1.head: عَدَّلَ
229.1.1.meaning: Addalahum: declared them just, that is trustworthy witnesses.

230.1.2-3.meaning: Abu Bakr: the first caliph, 11–13 AH (632–634 CE).

232.1.4-5.meaning: Jumada al-Akhira: the sixth month of the Islamic year.

232.2.3-4.meaning: “For seven remaining”: on the seventh night before the month's end.

233.1.2.head: الرِّدَّة
233.1.2.meaning: Al-Ridda: the Apostasy, the revolt of Arab tribes after the Prophet's death.

234.1.6.meaning: Umar: Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, 13–23 AH (634–644 CE).

234.2.4.meaning: Ghurar: blazes on horses' foreheads; days of glory.

235.2.3-4.meaning: “On their sneezers”: on their noses, in humiliation.

236.1.2.meaning: Kisra: Chosroes, the title of the Persian kings; here Yazdegerd III.

236.1.4.head: إيوان
236.1.4.meaning: Iwan: the great vaulted hall of the Persian kings at Ctesiphon.

238.1.3.head: الفاروق
238.1.3.meaning: Al-Faruq: “he who divides truth from falsehood”, Umar's title.

240.2.3-6.meaning: “O what a half”: a cry of wonder at all that happened in it.

241.1.2-4.meaning: Uthman ibn Affan: the third caliph, 23–35 AH (644–656 CE).

242.2.4-5.meaning: “Daughters of the roads”: little side paths; distractions and temptations.

243.1.4.meaning: Ali: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph, 35–40 AH (656–661 CE).

247.2.5.meaning: Safina: a freedman of the Prophet who reported, “The caliphate in my community will last thirty years, then there will be kingship.”

249.1.4.meaning: Mu'awiya: Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, founder of the Umayyad dynasty, 41–60 AH (661–680 CE).

251.1.4.meaning: Yazid: Yazid ibn Mu'awiya, 60–64 AH (680–683 CE).

252.1.2.meaning: Al-Husayn: the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (680 CE).

254.1.3.meaning: Mu'ayya: “little Mu'awiya”, Mu'awiya ibn Yazid, who ruled briefly in 64 AH (683 CE).

256.1.3-4.meaning: “Without a covenant”: without naming an heir.

257.1.4.meaning: Marwan: Marwan ibn al-Hakam, caliph 64–65 AH (684–685 CE).

258.1.2.meaning: Al-Dahhak: al-Dahhak ibn Qays, who led the Syrians for Ibn al-Zubayr.

258.2.1.head: راهِط
258.2.1.meaning: Rahit: Marj Rahit, a meadow near Damascus, where Marwan won his decisive battle.

260.1.3-4.meaning: Ibn al-Zubayr: Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, rival caliph in Mecca 64–73 AH (683–692 CE).

262.1.4.meaning: Al-Hajjaj: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, Abd al-Malik's general and later governor of Iraq.

263.2.1-2.meaning: The Battle of the Harra: Yazid's army defeated the people of Medina in 63 AH (683 CE) on the lava field east of the city.

264.1.2-5.meaning: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: Umayyad caliph, 65–86 AH (685–705 CE).

265.2.3.head: مُصعَب
265.2.3.meaning: Mus'ab: Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr, Abd Allah's brother and governor of Iraq.

268.1.4.meaning: Al-Walid: al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik, caliph 86–96 AH (705–715 CE).

270.1.2-5.meaning: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik: caliph 96–99 AH (715–717 CE).

271.2.3.head: دابِق
271.2.3.meaning: Dabiq: a village north of Aleppo, the camp for campaigns against the Byzantines.

271.2.4-5.meaning: “With his train let down”: at ease, in state.

272.1.5.meaning: Umar: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, caliph 99–101 AH (717–720 CE), famous for his justice.

273.2.1-2.meaning: Dayr Sim'an: “the monastery of Simeon”, near Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in Syria, where Umar died.

274.1.4.meaning: Yazid: Yazid II ibn Abd al-Malik, caliph 101–105 AH (720–724 CE).

277.1.4.meaning: Hisham: Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, caliph 105–125 AH (724–743 CE).

279.1.2-4.meaning: Al-Walid ibn Yazid: al-Walid II, caliph 125–126 AH (743–744 CE).

282.1.3.head: البَخراء
282.1.3.meaning: Al-Bakhra': a desert fortress near Palmyra.

283.1.2-5.meaning: Yazid ibn al-Walid al-Naqis: Yazid III, “the Reducer”, who cut the army's pay.

285.1.2.meaning: Marwan: Marwan II ibn Muhammad, the last Umayyad caliph, 127–132 AH (744–750 CE).

288.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Abbas: al-Saffah, the first Abbasid caliph, 132–136 AH (749–754 CE).

289.1.4-5.meaning: Banu al-Abbas: the Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas.

290.1.2-5.meaning: “The blade of kingship in its sheath”: power back where it belongs.

291.2.3.head: الكوفَة
291.2.3.meaning: Al-Kufa: a city in Iraq, centre of the Abbasid movement.

294.1.3.meaning: Al-Mansur: the second Abbasid caliph, 136–158 AH (754–775 CE), founder of Baghdad.

296.1.3.head: مُحرِم
296.1.3.meaning: Muhrim: in the state of consecration for pilgrimage.

296.2.2.meaning: Al-Mahdi: the third Abbasid caliph, 158–169 AH (775–785 CE).

298.1.2-3.meaning: Al-Hadi, Musa: the fourth Abbasid caliph, 169–170 AH (785–786 CE).

300.1.3.meaning: Al-Rashid: Harun al-Rashid, the fifth Abbasid caliph, 170–193 AH (786–809 CE).

302.2.1.head: طوس
302.2.1.meaning: Tus: a city in Khurasan, in north-eastern Iran, where al-Rashid died and was buried.

302.2.4-5.meaning: “The mountain fell”: a great man died.

303.1.2-3.meaning: Muhammad al-Amin: the sixth Abbasid caliph, 193–198 AH (809–813 CE).

307.1.2-4.meaning: Al-Ma'mun, Abd Allah: the seventh Abbasid caliph, 198–218 AH (813–833 CE).

309.2.2.head: البَذَندون
309.2.2.meaning: Al-Badhandun: a village a day's journey from Tarsus, in southern Anatolia.

310.1.3-4.meaning: Abu Ishaq: al-Mu'tasim, the eighth Abbasid caliph, 218–227 AH (833–842 CE).

311.1.1-2.meaning: Mu'tasiman bi-llah: “clinging to God”, also al-Mu'tasim's regnal title.

315.1.4.head: الواثِق
315.1.4.meaning: Al-Wathiq: the ninth Abbasid caliph, 227–232 AH (842–847 CE).

318.1.4.head: جَعفَر
318.1.4.meaning: Ja'far: al-Mutawakkil, the tenth Abbasid caliph, 232–247 AH (847–861 CE).

321.2.3.head: المَحَجَّة
321.2.3.meaning: Mahajja: the main road; the straight path of religion.

325.1.4.meaning: Al-Faraghina: Turkish troops from Farghana in Central Asia, the caliphs' guards at Samarra.

327.1.4.head: المُنتَصِر
327.1.4.meaning: Al-Muntasir: the eleventh Abbasid caliph, 247–248 AH (861–862 CE).

328.2.4.head: العَسكَر
328.2.4.meaning: Al-Askar: “the camp”, Samarra, built as a garrison city by al-Mu'tasim.

331.1.4.head: أَحمَد
331.1.4.meaning: Ahmad: al-Musta'in, the twelfth Abbasid caliph, 248–252 AH (862–866 CE).
